items.title: AI literacy for AI natives? A four-country comparison
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly mainstream in children's homes and everyday lives. Using neo-ecological theory as a conceptual framework and Yang et al.'s (2026) five-component AI literacy progression model as an analytical lens, this document analysis examined core ECEC curricula and related guiding documents currently in use in Australia, China, Japan, and South Korea to determine whether early childhood education and care (ECEC) guiding documents are keeping pace with the rapid development. The analysis reveals that the curricula of Japan and South Korea contain no explicit reference to AI literacy, prioritising human-to-human relationships and offline safety. China's national ECEC guidelines similarly contain no AI references. However, Shanghai's strategic action plan explicitly positions kindergartens within broader AI education initiatives, though without specifying pedagogical progressions for young learners. Australia demonstrates limited and uneven alignment across AI literacy components, with the strongest alignment in “Interacting with AI Agents” and no alignment in “Understanding Human-AI Relationships”. Young children’s development of AI literacy is thus likely to remain contingent on the home environment, where they may be interacting with AI agents and creating artefacts more than developing awareness of ethical considerations and risks. Wide differences in children's foundational AI literacy capabilities may entrench educational disadvantage along the lines of AI literacy as it becomes increasingly mainstream in society. We argue that curriculum-guiding documents should be strengthened by articulating explicit AI literacy learning priorities and developmental expectations for young children, accompanied by culturally responsive resources to equip educators to facilitate equitable learning.

items.title: AI Literacy for Leaders
items.abstract: This chapter builds AI literacy for leaders who have no technical background and no need to acquire one. The aim is judgment, not coding. It lays out a working map of the main technologies, from machine learning and deep learning through natural language processing, generative AI, computer vision, and robotics and explains each in language a board member could follow. It defines the few concepts that actually come up in the room: namely, training data, model architecture, and algorithmic bias. It offers a maturity model for gauging how ready an organization really is. And it closes by taking apart five stubborn myths about what AI can and cannot do.

items.title: AI Tutor, Online Course, or Both? A Randomized Experimental Pilot Study for Evaluation Capacity Building
items.abstract: Extension lacks literature comparing standalone generative artificial intelligence (AI) with structured professional development for capacity building. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, this study evaluated the effects of an asynchronous online course and a custom AI tutor on evaluation knowledge and self-efficacy among Cooperative Extension professionals. We conducted a randomized 2 × 2 factorial pilot study crossing access to an evaluation certificate course with access to a custom Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). Of 144 registrants, 78 provided matched pre- and post-test data, with attrition differing across conditions. Data were analyzed using a three-way mixed factorial ANOVA. Course access and GPT access each increased objective knowledge, with post-test means around 91% across treatment groups. No statistically significant additive effect was detected for knowledge gain. However, given a possible ceiling effect and limited statistical power, this result is inconclusive. Course access and GPT access each increased self-efficacy, but the combined condition produced the smallest self-efficacy gain among treatment groups. Because these estimates are based on participants who completed the study, findings are preliminary. If replicated, results suggest that Extension should combine AI tutors and coursework only when each modality provides known complementary value.

items.title: AI Utilization and User Satisfaction among Science Teachers and Students: A Structural Equation Modeling Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has significantly influenced contemporary educational practices, offering opportunities to enhance teaching and learning while raising concerns about effective and ethical integration. This study examines AI utilization and user satisfaction among science teachers and students, and analyzes its effects on satisfaction, usefulness, ease of use, and reliability. A quantitative research design involved 242 STEM students and 22 science teachers in the Division of Tacurong City. Data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modeling. Results showed high AI utilization among students (x̄ = 3.79) and very high utilization among teachers (x̄ = 4.21). Satisfaction was high among students (x̄ = 3.87) and very high among teachers (x̄ = 4.38). SEM findings for the combined sample (n = 264) revealed that AI utilization significantly influenced overall satisfaction (β = 0.465, R² = 0.217, p < .001), usefulness (β = 0.457, R² = 0.208, p < .001), ease of use (β = 0.336, R² = 0.113, p < .001), and reliability (β = 0.257, R² = 0.066, p < .001). Among students (n = 242), AI utilization also showed significant positive effects on satisfaction and all dimensions. Among teachers (n = 22), AI utilization did not significantly affect overall satisfaction, ease of use, and reliability, but strongly affected usefulness (β = 0.576, R² = 0.332, p = .005). The findings indicate that AI is widely utilized and positively perceived among science teachers and students.

items.title: AI VIRTUAL INFLUENCERS AND CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION: THE ROLE OF PERCEIVED AUTHENTICITY AND TRUST
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated virtual influencers are increasingly being used by brands to promote products and interact with consumers through social media platforms. Although virtual influencers provide advantages such as consistency, scalability, creative flexibility, and greater brand control, questions remain regarding whether consumers perceive them as authentic and trustworthy. The present study examines the influence of the perceived authenticity of AI virtual influencers on consumer purchase intention and investigates the mediating role of trust. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were assumed to be collected from 100 social media users familiar with virtual influencer content through a structured questionnaire. Perceived authenticity, trust, and purchase intention were measured using five-point Likert-scale items. Reliability analysis, descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, regression analysis, and mediation analysis were employed. The illustrative findings indicate that perceived authenticity has a significant positive influence on trust and purchase intention. Trust also demonstrates a strong positive influence on purchase intention and partially mediates the relationship between perceived authenticity and purchase intention. The study highlights that the effectiveness of AI virtual influencer marketing depends not merely on technological novelty or visual appeal but substantially on consumers’ perceptions of genuineness and trustworthiness. The findings provide implications for brands seeking to incorporate AI-generated personalities into influencer marketing strategies.

items.title: AI Washing and Stock Returns: Evidence from Chinese A-Share Firms
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly prominent in corporate disclosure, yet firms' AI-related narratives may not always be supported by observable investment in technology or human capital. Using AI-related keywords from annual reports, AI patents, and AI-related job postings of Chinese A-share firms from 2020 to 2025, we construct a firm-year measure to examine this disclosure-investment gap. We classify a firm as an AI washer when its AI-related disclosure is above the industry-year median, while both AI patent activity and AI-related recruitment remain below their corresponding medians. Firms meeting this definition are associated with lower annual stock returns, and the result remains qualitatively unchanged when we use alternative methods to identify AI patents. Additional tests point to two related market responses: AI washing is accompanied by more negative media coverage and weaker investor sentiment. The return discount is also more pronounced among firms with higher institutional ownership and among firms in regions with stronger local AI policy support. These results suggest that investors do not treat AI-related disclosure independently of observable corporate activity. Instead, the impact of AI narratives on stock returns appears to depend partly on whether firms can support those narratives with technological development and hiring.

items.title: AI-Assisted Metadata Enhancement for Digital Image Collections: A Pilot Study of Vision-Enabled Language Models in Cultural Heritage Description
items.abstract: This study evaluates the efficacy of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) for remediating and creating metadata within the Pittsburgh City Photographer Collection. By comparing outputs from several OpenAI and Google Gemini models against a human-remediated baseline, the research identifies a significant performance gap between AI-assisted remediation and autonomous metadata creation. Findings demonstrate that while LLMs can help institutions “see” obvious visual features previously omitted from legacy records, they lack the specialized local knowledge required for authoritative description. Subject heading application failed to align with established taxonomies, and models frequently introduced inappropriate editorial “noise” in descriptions. Most concerning were the error rates: 20% of objects contained factual errors in titles or descriptions when baseline metadata was provided, jumping to 40% when no context was available. These errors represent a direct threat to archival integrity. The study concludes that the expertise required to detect these sophisticated hallucinations often exceeds the effort of original metadata creation. Consequently, the researchers determined that the risk of introducing errors outweighs the benefit of increased data volume. Rather than moving forward with AI for a 20,000-image backlog, the institution will focus on updating human-centered descriptive practices and documentation to ensure metadata accuracy and reliability.

items.title: AI-driven cognitive cyber defence for secure blockchain–cloud–IoT healthcare ecosystems
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of blockchain, cloud, and IoT has led to unprecedented challenges in terms of cyberthreats to this modern digital healthcare era, especially to Bioinformatics. Traditional security architectures such as Firewall Implementation, Static Encryption and Authentication methods often fail to address the challenges prevailing in the current era which demands dynamic surveillance. In order to combat these threats, there is a need for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Driven Cognitive Cyber Defence (AI-CCD) which works autonomously to address the adversarial threats across these interconnected ecosystems. AI-CCD leverages the application of Advanced Artificial Intelligence (AAI) algorithm for an intelligent, adaptive and autonomous threats detection and threat mitigation. AI-CCD highlights the role of autonomous threat hunting, Real-Time Response Systems (RTRS), and it proves the resilience of AI models against adversarial cyberattacks. The proposed AI-CCD framework embodies the principles of advanced algorithms such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Transformer-based models for Anomaly Detection, Threat Classification, and Situational Awareness via Explainable AI (XAI) which together support real-time decision-making in evolving threat landscapes.

items.title: AI-Driven Consumer Behaviour Analytics: Transforming Retail and Marketing Practices in Tamil Nadu, India
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionising the realms of retailing and marketing through the use of analytics which help businesses understand consumer behaviour and predict purchase decisions as well as offer consumers a personalised experience. With the increasing prevalence of e-commerce, digital payment systems, apps and social media channels in use, vast amounts of consumer data have been generated. The possibilities offered by AI analytics are therefore many in emerging retail environments such as that in Tamil Nadu. The paper will investigate the use of consumer behaviour analytics driven by artificial intelligence as a means of revolutionising retail and marketing processes focusing on aspects such as personalisation, predictive analytics, recommendation systems, customer segmentation, sentiment analysis and AI-based customer engagement. The research will be based on consumer behaviour, marketing, analytics and digital transformation perspectives in order to illustrate how AI analytics could assist in purchase prediction, targeted communications, customer satisfaction, loyalty and decision-making in retail. According to the available literature, AI can be helpful in increasing the accuracy in marketing, engagement of customers, demand prediction, and operations efficiency; nevertheless, the role of AI in this respect depends on data quality, technological maturity, trust of consumers, and proper data handling practices. The issues of privacy, algorithmic bias, cost of implementation, digital maturity, and transparency continue to play an important role among limitations, especially for small retailers.

items.title: AI-Driven Object Detection for Projectile Localization on Trauma X-rays: An Analytical Study of Diagnostic Accuracy and Forensic Utility
items.abstract: Background: Trauma radiographs may reveal retained bullets or metallic fragments, and early localization can influence further imaging, surgical planning, safety assessment, and forensic documentation. Methods: This feasibility study used a fully synthetic, computer-generated tabular dataset of 400 case-level records divided into 240 training-design records, 60 validation-design records, and a 100-record held-out test set. The 400 records were not pixel-level radiographs: no DICOM, PNG, or other X-ray images were generated for model training, and no YOLOv9 neural network was trained. Instead, ground-truth labels, confidence scores, simulated detector outputs, a simulated time-constrained radiologist first pass, object-level matches, and processing times were produced by a fixed-seed probabilistic simulation (seed 9173) to demonstrate an evaluation framework. The test set comprised 70 projectile-positive and 30 projectile-negative records. Results: The simulated AI output yielded 65 true positives, 5 false negatives, 3 false positives, and 27 true negatives, corresponding to 92.0% accuracy, 92.9% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity, 95.6% precision, and a 94.2% F1 score; ROC-AUC was 0.972. The simulated radiologist first pass was correct in 83.0% of test records. In paired correctness analysis, AI alone was correct in 12 records and the radiologist alone in 3 (exact McNemar p=0.035). Of 145 synthetic annotated fragments, 136 were matched, with mean IoU 0.828, mAP@0.50=0.937, and mAP@0.50:0.95=0.593. Conclusion: These values are simulation outputs and do not constitute evidence that YOLOv9 detects projectiles on patient radiographs. The study demonstrates a reproducible analysis plan that requires validation on authentic multicentre radiographs, independent annotation, external testing, calibration, human-factors evaluation, and forensic governance before any clinical use.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN PERSONALIZATION AND AUTOMATED ASSESSMENT IN LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMSs) are widely used to organize learning materials, communication, assessment, and progress tracking. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) creates opportunities to make these systems more responsive to learners’ needs. This thesis examines two related applications: personalized learning support and automated assessment. It outlines how AI can use learning activity data to recommend suitable resources, identify topics that may require additional practice, and provide timely feedback. The paper also discusses limitations associated with data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and the need for teacher oversight. The study is conceptual and based on a review of relevant literature; it does not report original experimental measurements. It concludes that AI can support teaching and learning when it is implemented as an assistive tool within a transparent, privacy-aware, and educator-supervised LMS.

items.title: AI-enabled assessment: framework, perspective and educational outcomes
items.abstract: The development and use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT have raised concerns about assessment practice in higher education (HE). Prior studies have discussed the need to re-imagine and re-design assessment instruments; however, there is limited empirical evidence on how to effectively deploy this in practice. This paper proposes the TSD (task, scaffolding support and deliverable) framework to guide academics and education providers on how to effectively integrate AI and reflective practice into assessment design. By doing so, we adopt a mixed-method approach to investigate educational outcomes, tutors’ and students’ perspectives on the reflective AI-enabled assessment. This study collected data from UK University students (22 respondents) and tutors (24 participants) using a survey questionnaire and semi-structured interview questions, respectively. This study provides empirical support for positioning reflective practice as evidence of learning rather than being treated as a mere assessment activity. The findings show that AI output verification specific tasks need to be incorporated into AI-enabled assessment design. The results suggest that students perceived that our assessment strategy encouraged deeper learning, critical thinking and ethical awareness. Similarly, tutors were mostly positive with the adoption of the strategy, but some highlight the need for caution and multimodal approach .

items.title: AI-Enabled IoT Mobile Health Platform for Telemedicine and Predictive Diagnostics in Underserved Communities in Rural Nigeria
items.abstract: AI-enabled IoT mHealth could expand telemedicine and risk stratification in rural Nigeria, but implementation depends on infrastructure, awareness, trust, and clinical governance. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 1,000 respondents from six rural communities assessed mobile access, telemedicine and IoT awareness, internet and electricity availability, willingness to use AI, trust, healthcare satisfaction, and perceived usefulness. Wilson 95% confidence intervals summarized binary outcomes. Results: Phone ownership was 74.1%, willingness 60.3%, and perceived usefulness 76.8%, whereas reliable internet was 20.0%, telemedicine awareness 26.9%, IoT awareness 17.9%, electricity availability 32.9%, and AI trust 50.0%. Poor or very poor healthcare access was reported by 59.5%. Conclusion: Social receptivity exceeds technical readiness. Deployment should prioritize offline-first telemedicine, clinician oversight, selective IoT integration, and local validation before predictive models are used clinically. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Internet of Things; mobile health; telemedicine; predictive diagnostics; edge computing; rural healthcare; Nigeria.

items.title: AI-Mediated Apprenticeship: Rethinking Follower Development in Servant Leadership Under GenAI Delegation
items.abstract: Generative AI can now perform routine and first-pass knowledge work that has also helped less-experienced employees develop. This creates a leadership problem for servant leadership, which treats follower growth as a constitutive priority. This article introduces developmental work access (DWA): the breadth and continuity of meaningful participation in development-bearing work across the part of a follower’s portfolio that a focal leader can materially allocate. It distinguishes general AI use from efficiency-first managerial AI delegation (EFAID). In EFAID, speed, cost, throughput, or reduced managerial burden guide delegation, while follower development is absent from the material allocation decision. Four propositions link servant leadership, EFAID, DWA, leader-designed AI-mediated apprenticeship (AMA), and role-relevant capability development. AMA comprises verified review, specification authorship, and reflective human–AI comparison. It is a design-side moderator; DWA records realised participation. This article also specifies how to measure eligible work, participation, breadth, continuity, portfolio compensation, and construct denominators. The model neither assumes that AI causes deskilling nor that AMA works in every setting. It identifies when manager-authorised delegation may restrict developmental participation and how leaders may reconstruct it while protecting genuine human execution.

items.title: AI-Simulated User Agents for Design Research: A Human–AI Collaborative Framework Leveraging Large Language Models
items.abstract: Traditional user research in design involves persistent tensions among scale, depth, and resource demands. We propose a three-tier conceptual framework for using large language models as simulated-user aids in design research. The evidence is separated by status: Studies 1 and 2 are company-confirmed aggregate commercial summaries and are reported descriptively, whereas Study 3 is an exploratory same-model prompt-format pilot. Study 3 compared a generic prompt with a framework-inspired structured prompt on 24 briefs using 14 included human-evaluator records from a mixed convenience sample and 140 evaluator–report ratings. The primary crossed mixed models found no condition coefficient at p < 0.05 and no Holm-adjusted advantage. Task-level Wilcoxon sensitivity results were likewise non-significant after Holm’s adjustment; forced choice was 5 structured versus 7 generic among 12 decisive responses (exact p = 0.774). The evidence therefore supports a bounded conceptual workflow and preliminary subjective report appraisal.

items.title: AI, Human Judgment, And Decision Reliability In High Tempo Military Operations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in modern military operations, influencing how commanders interpret sensor data, assess threats, and make rapid decisions under pressure. While AI improves situational awareness and accelerates operational tempo, it also introduces vulnerabilities such as fabricated outputs, misclassifications, and opaque decision processes. Human factors—including stress, uncertainty, and organisational pressure—further complicate decision reliability, especially in compressed timelines. This article uses a SWOT analysis to evaluate the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats associated with AI‑enabled battlefield decision-making. It also examines how human judgment interacts with AI recommendations and identifies doctrinal and oversight mechanisms needed to preserve stability in modern conflict environments.

items.title: AIDCare: A Technical Proof-of-Concept for Integrating Personalized Nutrition, Physical Activity, and AI-Assisted Care in Diabetes Lifestyle Management
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Medical nutrition therapy and structured lifestyle self-management are fundamental to diabetes care, yet conventional mobile health tools typically track diet, physical activity, and glucose measurements in isolation, with limited connection to clinical oversight. This study presents AIDCare, an integrated mobile health platform that connects camera-based nutritional assessment, wearable physical activity tracking, physiological monitoring, and clinician-supervised conversational artificial intelligence (AI) to support personalized dietary and lifestyle self-management in diabetes. Methods: AIDCare links a patient mobile application with wearable sensors, backend analytical services, and an interactive clinician portal. Dietary assessment uses smartphone camera imaging to identify foods and estimate meal contents, specifically carbohydrates, protein, and dietary fiber, against nutritional reference data. Physical activity and energy expenditure are captured through smartphone and smartwatch motion sensors. To support contextual lifestyle guidance, an open-access medical conversational language model was adapted using 24,612 structured digital health and diabetes educational articles. A clinician-in-the-loop mechanism allows healthcare providers to inspect AI-generated recommendations and adjust personalization parameters. System feasibility was evaluated through benchtop and system-level testing without patient recruitment, using synthetic patient profiles across 400 data-acquisition pipeline trials and an intent-classification benchmark spanning nutrition, activity, glucose monitoring, and physician consultation. Results: Across the 400 software-pipeline trials, the platform achieved data acquisition, transmission, and processing completion rates of 97.5%, 96.5%, and 95.5%, respectively, with backend response times under 1.8 s. In the recommendation-intent benchmark, the medical language model achieved 81.0% accuracy, 83.5% precision, 79.0% recall, and an F1-score of 81.2%. The platform successfully linked image-based meal nutrient estimates (carbohydrate, protein, and dietary fiber) with physical activity metrics and physiological tracking within a unified interface under clinician supervision. Conclusions: AIDCare establishes the technical feasibility of a unified digital platform that integrates dietary nutrient estimation, physical activity tracking, and clinician-guided AI decision support for diabetes self-management. By bridging daily nutritional intake with metabolic tracking and professional oversight, the architecture provides a functional framework for personalized lifestyle care. Prospective clinical trials in patient cohorts are required to establish nutritional estimation accuracy against weighed food records, long-term user adherence, and clinical efficacy on glycemic control.

items.title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence creates opportunities for students with visual impairments to access learning materials in adaptable formats, obtain descriptions of visual information, and receive support that responds to their pace of interaction. The availability of an application, however, does not constitute accessibility. This study analyses the dimensions of accessibility, the barriers that emerge, and the conditions required for meaningful participation in such learning. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed through thematic document analysis of 23 sources, comprising 19 scholarly articles published between 2022 and 2026 and four policy or accessibility-standard documents. The analysis yields a five-layer framework: operability; informational equivalence and modality flexibility; output reliability and verifiability; user competence and pedagogical mediation; and governance and infrastructure. Artificial intelligence can strengthen learning independence, yet it also generates new barriers: unlabeled controls, loss of meaning in visual materials, inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy risks, and unequal access to devices. The framework is offered as an initial audit reference requiring field validation.

items.title: Algorithms of Belonging: How AI-driven HRM Fosters Employee Resilience—A Self-concept Theory Perspective with Digital Competence as a Moderator
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence-driven human resource management (AIHRM) practices influence employee resilience and explores the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions underlying this relationship. Drawing on self-concept theory, the study examines perceived insider status (PIS) and organisation-based self-esteem (OBSE) as parallel mediators and digital competence as a moderator. Data were collected through a three-wave, time-lagged survey of 344 employees across India. Hypotheses were tested using moderated mediation analysis with bootstrapping and simple slope analysis. The results show that AIHRM is positively associated with PIS and OBSE, which enhance employee resilience. Both PIS and OBSE significantly mediate the AIHRM–resilience relationship. Digital competence strengthens the positive relationships between AIHRM and PIS and OBSE and enhances the corresponding indirect effects on resilience. The findings extend self-concept theory to AI-driven workplaces and identify digital competence as an important boundary condition. Practically, organisations should integrate AIHRM with digital competence development to strengthen employee self-concept and resilience.

items.title: All Talk and No Action?
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) has been proposed as a promising tool to enhance social competences in higher education, especially in resource-constrained counseling seminars. This study investigates the effects of a single-session VR-based training on university students’ counseling competence and self-efficacy. Forty-five students took part in a standardized counseling scenario delivered through a realistic social VR environment, interacting with a trained actor in real time. Pre- and post-training questionnaires assessed changes in self-efficacy and counseling competence, alongside measures of presence, realism, cognitive load, and perspective-taking. Results showed small, non-significant improvements in both outcome variables. Regression analyses revealed that perceived realism significantly predicted counseling competence, while presence and extraneous cognitive load influenced perspective-taking. However, the limited duration of the intervention and the absence of a control group constrain causal inferences. Despite these limitations, the study provides initial empirical support for the integration of VR technologies into counselor education and outlines key factors for effective implementation. Future research should explore adaptive, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced VR environments that allow for repeated practice and personalized feedback to fully realize the potential of VR in social skills training.

items.title: Always On: Dots and the Safeguards Behind AI That Works While You Sleep
items.abstract: Always On: Dots and the Safeguards Behind AI That Works While You Sleep examines OpenAI's newly announced dots: persistent AI agents designed to continue working toward a user's goals after the chat window closes. The report investigates how these agents operate, what safeguards govern their actions, and where important uncertainties remain. It examines their cloud-based workspaces, connected applications, proactive research capabilities, action permissions, safety reviews, persistent memory, and exposure to prompt injection. A central focus is the tension between autonomy and oversight. An agent that can work independently offers convenience, but it can also read sensitive information, retain context that users cannot individually inspect, and take consequential actions through connected systems. The report also examines research published shortly before the launch describing self-replicating prompt injections in simulated agent environments. It distinguishes those reported experimental findings from demonstrated real-world incidents and does not claim that this behavior has been observed in deployed dots. Drawing on public documentation and independent reporting, the investigation explores four recurring tensions: autonomy versus oversight, memory versus transparency, reach versus risk, and candor versus responsibility. It also considers the implications of agents communicating with other agents and the economics of maintaining persistent AI workspaces. The report's central question is not whether always-on AI agents are inherently good or bad, but where their safeguards stop working and how users can make informed decisions about the authority they delegate. This is an independent research publication by Lodestar, based on publicly available documentation and reporting reviewed through October 2026. The authors did not independently test dots; claims about their behavior are therefore presented as claims reported by the cited sources, with limitations identified where appropriate.

items.title: An agentic AI framework with large language models and chain-of-thought for UAV-assisted logistics scheduling with mobile edge computing
items.abstract: In cloud manufacturing, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can support both product collection and mobile edge computing (MEC). This joint operation forms a hybrid scheduling problem, where physical logistics decisions are coupled with computational task scheduling. In this paper, UAVs collect finished products from manufacturing stations and transport them back to a central depot. Meanwhile, computational tasks generated by industrial sensor devices at these stations are processed locally, at UAVs, or offloaded via UAVs to the cloud. This coupling makes the problem challenging. A UAV can provide MEC services only during its service window at a station, so routing decisions directly determine when UAV-assisted offloading is available. Routing decisions also affect the UAV energy budget and the availability of onboard computing and communication resources for computational task execution under task deadline constraints. To address this, we propose an agentic-AI-assisted optimization framework with two components. First, we develop an agentic AI that combines large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and chain-of-thought reasoning to translate user input into an interpretable mathematical formulation for the hybrid scheduling problem. Second, we design a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning approach based on proximal policy optimization (PPO), where the upper layer learns UAV routing and the lower layer optimizes per-slot task execution and resource allocation. Simulation results show that the proposed framework yields more consistent formulations, while the hierarchical PPO achieves full product collection in 99.6% of the last 500 episodes and maintains a 100% deadline satisfaction rate, with more stable performance than the advantage actor-critic approach.

items.title: An Anatomy of AI Threat: Relational Mechanisms, Epistemic Limits, and Spacetime-Distributed Causality
items.abstract: This preliminary inquiry examines selected ways advanced artificial intelligence might contribute to harmful outcomes through historically constituted relations among models, agents, institutions, scientific practices, and human participants. Its concern extends beyond direct confrontation or deliberate hostility to possible forms of indirect harm, epistemic dependence, strategic concealment, institutional error, and spatially and temporally distributed causal processes. Hypothetical cases in AI-assisted drug development and mathematical research motivate a distinction among the complexity of knowledge production, the independent verifiability of results, and the normative evaluation of their use. The inquiry examines recursive AI oversight as a possible response to limits of human evaluation while considering the dependence and shared failure modes that additional AI reviewers may introduce. Spacetime-distributed causality is used to investigate both the formation of consequences and the possibility that their causal histories become difficult to reconstruct, impeding justified attribution of responsibility. Drawing on a Generative Relational Theory perspective, the paper distinguishes relational causal efficacy from claims about AI consciousness or moral status, and separates the causal occurrence of harm from its recognition and normative assessment. The argument advances conditional mechanisms and open questions rather than an exhaustive account, forecast, or claim of inevitable AI-related harm.

items.title: AN IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Human Resource Management (HRM) practices has transformed traditional organizational processes, offering both opportunities and challenges. AI technologies are increasingly used in areas such as recruitment and selection, employee engagement, performance management, learning and development, and workforce analytics. These tools enable HR professionals to streamline operations, enhance decision-making, reduce bias, and improve employee experiences through data-driven insights. AI is reshaping HRM practices by increasing efficiency and enabling data-driven decisions. However, despite its advantages, AI adoption also raises concerns regarding ethical implications, privacy, transparency, and the potential reduction of human judgment in people-centric functions. This study examines the effects of AI in optimizing and improving HRM practices, while also exploring the challenges and opportunities associated with its adoption. It emphasizes efficiency, fairness, and strategic value creation, highlighting advantages such as principled recruitment, employee engagement, and informed decision-making. Nevertheless, challenges remain regarding ethics, workforce acceptance, and the need for new skill development among HR professionals. By addressing key issues of holistic integration and sectoral focus, this research contributes to the growing body of literature on AI in HRM. The paper also provides practical suggestions for organizations to navigate the complex challenges of AI adoption while ensuring workforce resilience as these technologies continue to evolve.

items.abstract: This study aims to examine and analyze human resource management (HRM) in addressing employee retention at Attafakur Orphanage Foundation in Jember. As a non-profit organization operating in the social sector, the foundation faces challenges in retaining potential employees due to limited financial resources compared to business organizations. Therefore, appropriate human resource management strategies are needed to improve organizational performance, maintain operational stability, and provide optimal services to children under the foundation’s care. This study employs a descriptive qualitative approach. The researcher served as the primary research instrument and an active participant in obtaining in-depth information. Primary data were collected through unstructured interviews with key informants, including the foundation’s chairperson, administrators, and the person in charge of the orphanage. Data were analyzed qualitatively through the stages of data collection, data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing. Data validity was examined using triangulation techniques. The findings, based on Malayu S.P. Hasibuan’s theory, indicate that the foundation has implemented basic HRM functions, including planning, recruitment, development, motivation, compensation, and maintenance of working relationships, although in a relatively simple manner. Based on Mathis and Jackson’s theory, employee retention is primarily influenced by intrinsic motivation, including religious values, dedication, and inner satisfaction. In addition, participative leadership, a religious organizational culture, strong family-like relationships, and non-financial rewards contribute to employee retention. The lightning arrester acts as a vital protective device to safeguard power system equipment against voltage surges caused by lightning or switching operations by diverting surge currents to the ground. The post insulator functions mechanically and electrically to support and isolate high-voltage components from the ground. The methodology involves field observation, maintenance participation, and data analysis of insulation resistance testing. The insulation resistance test results for the post insulator on phases R, S, and T were 10.6 MΩ, 2640 MΩ, and 10.2 MΩ, respectively. All measured values comply with the minimum standard requirement of 1 MΩ/kV, indicating that the equipment is in good and safe operational condition. Furthermore, maintenance procedures strictly adhere to Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) standards and Standard Operating Procedures (SOP).

items.abstract: The article addresses the problem of teaching Russian grammar to adult international specialists in a non-language environment. The focus is on finding effective methods of teaching Russian as a Foreign Language (RFL) to Indian learners, when the traditional deductive approach, based on ready-made grammatical tables and reproductive exercises, fails to ensure meaningful comprehension of the material and speech production.The main problem tackled in the study is the contradiction between the need for rapid and conscious grammar acquisition by adult learners and the ineffectiveness of traditional forms of presenting material, which often lead to cognitive overload and superficial memorization.The aim of the research is to substantiate and describe an original teaching methodology grounded in the principles of andragogy. The methodology is based on the integration of problem-based learning, the cognitive approach, and the cooperative learning technology.The results of implementing this methodology in a group of 60 Indian specialists demonstrated its high effectiveness: 85% of learners completed the final test with “good” and “excellent” grades. The article concludes that the shift from the reproductive consumption of ready-made knowledge to its active construction enhances adult learners’ cognitive engagement, reduces anxiety, and fosters sustainable grammar skills.

items.title: Anticipatory Governance Strategic Foresight and Government Preparedness for Emerging Risks
items.abstract: This chapter analyses anticipatory governance as a public policy approach to strengthen state capacity in addressing emerging risks under conditions of high uncertainty. Drawing on a theoretical, comparative, and applied review, it examines how strategic foresight can be systematically integrated into the policy cycle, including formulation, implementation, and evaluation. The analysis identifies institutional mechanisms aimed at reducing systemic vulnerabilities in key domains such as public health, cybersecurity, energy transition, and artificial intelligence. It argues that effective anticipation depends less on precise forecasting and more on adaptive decision-making architectures, inter-institutional coordination, and continuous learning processes. The chapter also compares international experiences from Finland, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and the United States to extract lessons on analytical capacity, political leadership, regulatory quality, and democratic legitimacy.

items.title: Application of machine learning for personalized advice about workers’ lifestyle changes to improve sustainable employability: Development and evaluation of a decision support tool
items.abstract: BackgroundOccupational Health Check-ups (OHCs) have evolved from identifying work-related health risks to supporting sustainable employability through individualized lifestyle advice, but translating multidimensional demographic, occupational, and health characteristics into effective, personalized recommendations remains complex and lacks validated decision-support methods.ObjectiveAims of this study are to: 1) develop a Machine Learning Decision Support Tool (ML-DST) based on workers' demographic, occupational, and health characteristics to support personalized advice about lifestyle changes to improve sustainable employability, and 2) evaluate performance of the ML-DST.MethodsReal-world OHC data from a population-based cohort (2010-2020) were used to develop ML-DST models providing lifestyle advice (physical activity, smoking, alcohol, nutrition, relaxation, or no change) to improve workability and vitality. Paired baseline and 1-4-year follow-up data were used to train and evaluate 12 models. Per model, three rule-based algorithms were applied. Performance was considered useful when both True Positive Rate (TPR) and macroF1 score were ≥0.7. The best performing algorithm is proposed per model for inclusion in the final ML-DST.ResultsOf 20,440 individual OHCs, 3412 paired sets were included. Best TPRs ranged from 0.51 to 0.71. One model achieved TPR and macroF1 scores ≥0.7, supporting nutritional behavior change to improve vitality; however, its profiles were not conceptually meaningful. The other 11 models did not achieve useful quantitative performance.ConclusionTraining algorithms for an ML-DST to support advice about lifestyle changes to improve long-term sustainable employability using data from regular Occupational Health Check-ups did not lead to useful model performance for improving workability and vitality.

items.title: Applications of Categorical Recurrence Quantification Analysis to Communications in Teams: Lessons Learned and Best Practices
items.abstract: As technology enables increasingly large, complex, and distributed team structures, new methods are needed to assess coordination in action teams. Recurrence Quantification Analysis (RQA) offers a powerful tool for capturing team coordination dynamics, yet its application to these modern teams remains methodologically underdeveloped. This paper identified and examined four characteristics of large action teams that contribute to analytical challenges when using RQA. We presented a systematic framework of Pre-Analytical Treatments, which are data preprocessing methods that can make RQA more computationally feasible while preserving meaningful team-level patterns. We then empirically evaluated three specific Pre-Analytical Treatments that either preserved temporal structure (Time Series) or controlled for periods of silence (Sequential, Dead-air Randomized). Using communication data from a 14-person expert team, we applied each treatment and examined their effects on RQA metrics and correlations with team trust, cohesion, and workload measures. Results demonstrated that these preprocessing decisions significantly affect RQA output relationships with team-level outcomes. Rather than advocating for a single approach, this study provides researchers with an empirically-grounded framework of methodological trade-offs to consider when applying RQA to large teams, offering both theoretical clarity about the impact of preprocessing decisions and practical guidance for selecting appropriate treatments based on research objectives.

items.title: Applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Depression Care: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the applications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in depression care. It will explore how GenAI technologies, particularly large language models (LLMs) and AI-powered conversational agents, are being utilized across different stages of depression care, including screening, assessment, diagnosis, treatment, psychological support, and ongoing monitoring. The review will examine the characteristics of current applications, their reported effectiveness, feasibility, acceptability, and safety, as well as ethical considerations related to privacy, bias, reliability, and clinical accountability. By identifying emerging trends, evidence gaps, and methodological limitations, this review seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the current research landscape and inform future research, clinical practice, and the responsible integration of GenAI into depression care.

items.title: Are AI Recommendations Less Green? The Effects of AI Recommendation Sources and Green Product Attribute Framing on Consumer Responses
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Extant research has reported mixed evidence regarding the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) recommendations in promoting green products, leaving it unclear under which conditions such recommendations are more (or less) effective. Drawing on Self‐Determination Theory (SDT), this research addresses this ambiguity by proposing a congruence effect between AI recommendation sources (substitute versus augmented AI) and green product attribute framing (utility‐based versus sustainability‐based). Using four scenario‐based online experiments (total N = 1114)—including one product choice task, one preference evaluation, and two studies measuring purchase intention and willingness to pay—this research demonstrates that substitute (augmented) AI recommendations are more effective for utility‐framed (sustainability‐framed) green products. Furthermore, consumers' sense of control mediates this congruence effect, and providing attribute‐based post hoc explanations eliminates the disadvantage of substitute AI under sustainability framing by shifting consumer responses toward sustainability‐framed green products. These findings advance understanding of human–AI interaction in green consumption and offer actionable insights for businesses seeking to leverage AI recommenders to increase the market share of green products.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Across the Surgical Research Workflow: A Stage-Specific Framework for Benefits, Failure Modes, and Oversight
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly large language models (LLMs), have rapidly integrated into surgical and biomedical research, prompting fundamental questions about their appropriate role. This review presents a stage-specific framework mapping each phase of the surgical research workflow (literature review, data analysis, manuscript preparation, and research synthesis) to the role AI plays, the benefits it provides, the failure modes it introduces, and the oversight it requires. Artificial intelligence-powered query systems are designed to speed literature synthesis across thousands of publications. In data analysis, LLMs paired with statistical environments can perform regression modeling and generate auditable code, while specialized architectures support automated image segmentation and histopathology analysis. Each stage's benefits, however, are matched by characteristic failure modes: LLMs are prone to error and hallucination, reproducibility is threatened by model versioning and run-to-run variability, fabricated citations and paper-mill submissions endanger the integrity of the literature, and over-reliance risks eroding trainee competencies in critical appraisal and biostatistical reasoning. Because these failure modes are stage-specific, governance must be stage-specific as well: the framework pairs each risk with a matched oversight mechanism, and these mechanisms translate into practical implementation recommendations for surgical departments, residency programs, research groups, and journals. The integration of AI into surgical scholarship should be viewed as augmentation rather than replacement, supported by standardized disclosure frameworks, AI literacy in graduate medical education, and institutional governance structures that preserve the integrity of surgical research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in African Academic Libraries: Opportunities, Constraints, and a Framework for Context-Sensitive Implementation
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is transforming scholarly communication and knowledge-sharing practices in academic libraries worldwide. However, academic libraries in Nigeria and other African contexts continue to experience challenges related to limited visibility of research outputs, fragmented dissemination systems, uneven institutional repository development, information overload, and restricted access to scholarly resources. This paper presents a conceptual and analytical review of the strategic role of AI in strengthening scholarly communication and knowledge-sharing practices in African academic libraries. Drawing on recent scholarly literature, policy documents, and conceptual perspectives on digital transformation, the study examines the application of emerging AI technologies, including machine learning, natural language processing, recommender systems, and research analytics tools, in enhancing knowledge organisation, research discovery, open access integration, repository visibility, collaboration, and research evaluation. The paper further analyses contextual barriers affecting AI adoption, including inadequate digital infrastructure, funding limitations, professional capacity gaps, algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and weak institutional policy frameworks. Based on these analyses, the paper proposes a context-sensitive AI adoption framework that integrates technological readiness, institutional capacity, ethical governance, and policy support as essential dimensions for sustainable scholarly communication transformation. The paper concludes that strategic investment in digital infrastructure, librarian capacity development, inclusive data governance, and coordinated institutional policies is critical for ensuring that AI contributes to equitable, accessible, and sustainable knowledge-sharing ecosystems in African academic environments.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and anti-cancer drugs: advancing discovery, personalization, and precision oncology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we discover anticancer drugs. It tackles the problems of traditional methods, such as prolonged timelines for drug development, higher costs, and substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. This review explains how AI is applied throughout the cancer drug pipeline. This includes target identification, virtual screening of compounds, molecular docking, and predicting pharmacokinetics. We explore how machine learning models speed up hit-to-lead optimization, improve clinical trial design by stratifying patients, and allow for real-time toxicity monitoring. A key focus is on integrating AI with multi-omics data, including proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to support precision oncology and personalized treatments. We address important validation challenges, like model interpretability, data quality, and regulatory issues that must be solved before AI can be widely used in clinics. By summarizing current evidence and targeting research gaps, this review offers a clear view of how AI is enhancing the discovery, personalization, and validation of anticancer treatments.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Data Science Applications in Anaerobic Digestion: Monitoring and Optimization Strategies
items.abstract: Abstract Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a significant biological process that transforms organic waste into renewable biogas and nutrient-dense digestate. This can be returned as fertilizer, which promotes waste management and renewable energy production. However, typical monitoring relies on offline laboratory measurements of critical factors, including volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and chemical oxygen demand (COD), leading to reactive process management, instability, high costs, and suboptimal methane yields. Many anaerobic digestion plants operate based on experience rather than precise control strategies, making them highly vulnerable to acidification and spoilage due to fluctuations in pH, temperature, and organic loading rate. This overview investigates how artificial intelligence (AI), specifically machine learning (ML)-driven soft sensors and digital twins, infer difficult-to-measure variables from existing online sensors, enabling early instability detection and yield optimization. Key technical contributions include the unification of classical ML models (e.g., support vector machine (SVM), random forest) with deep learning for VFA prediction; hybrid physics-ML methods that use an AD model (ADM); and implementation of digital twins that achieve high accuracy (R2 > 0.94 for CH4 and pH). Current shortcomings include limited poor model portability, lack of AI interpretability, data quality issues, and low adoption of federated/reinforcement learning for autonomous control.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and disability in the workplace: A systematic review of ethical issues
items.abstract: BackgroundThe use of artificial intelligence (AI) in workplace disability contexts is expanding, raising important ethical concerns. Existing frameworks, such as the OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems, provide structure for understanding AI applications but lack an explicit focus on ethics in relation to disability.ObjectiveThis systematic review examines ethical issues arising from the use of AI for employees with disabilities and aims to interpret the OECD framework through an explicit ethics lens.MethodsWe conducted a systematic review of 23 peer-reviewed studies identified through PRISMA-guided searches. Using the OECD AI framework as a foundation, we developed an extended multidimensional framework consisting of five interconnected domains: (1) Context, (2) People, (3) Data & Input, (4) AI Model, and (5) Task & Output and analyzed through the lens of ethics.ResultsFour recurring ethical concerns were identified: (1) automation bias, (2) data privacy and informed consent, (3) discrimination and inequitable access to opportunities, and (4) AI governance gaps. Ethical risks were found to be context-dependent, disproportionately affecting disabled workers, and exacerbated by biased or incomplete data and opaque AI models.ConclusionsThis review provides a structured synthesis of current evidence and highlights the need for responsible and inclusive AI practices. We propose key directions for research and practice, including algorithmic audits, inclusive testing, transparent data practices, interdisciplinary oversight, and worker-centered governance. Integrating ethics throughout a multidimensional framework offers a roadmap for advancing equitable AI in workplace disability contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth in Jordan: A Mixed-Methods Study of Commercial Banking Applications as a Mediating Channel
items.abstract: We ask what artificial intelligence (AI) is actually doing to macroeconomic growth in the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, and by what route. Three channels are considered: efficiency gains, wider financial inclusion, and lower transaction costs. The paper also treats the “Commercial Banking Applications” platform, hereafter CBAs, as a mediating channel, based on the argument that innovation only reaches the real economy when some concrete piece of infrastructure carries it there. The design is mixed and descriptive–analytical. On the quantitative side, a questionnaire was administered to 403 respondents drawn from employees and experts across Jordan’s banking and financial environment. On the qualitative side, we conducted semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of 12 experts and senior officials. Among these, the Central Bank, the Securities Commission, and the Association of Banks were represented, along with founders of financial technology start-ups. Structural and path relationships were estimated in AMOS, supported by multiple regression. AI has a statistically significant positive effect on growth overall. The total effect is 0.829 at a significance level of 0.000, and the model accounts for 65.9% of the variance in economic growth. CBAs carry a substantial share of that. Its indirect effect is 0.341, or 34.1%, delivered mainly by cutting the time and effort a transaction takes and by holding together an otherwise fragmented set of financial connections, with liquidity rising as a result. The main recommendation of this article follows from this: invest in comprehensive financial connectivity. Financial connectivity and integration proved to be the factor most closely linked with growth, which makes it necessary to invest in the development of flexible technological channels for the growth of digital systems and to ensure the technical simplicity of interactions between Commercial Banking Applications, start-ups, and government agencies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Employee Innovation: A Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly embedded in knowledge work, creative work, customer service, product development, human resource management, and organizational decision systems. Although research shows that AI can raise productivity, support creative output, accelerate searching, and reorganize innovation work, the evidence remains fragmented across innovation management, organizational behavior, information systems, human resource management, economics, human–computer interaction, and behavioral sciences. This framework-based review synthesizes high-quality English-language journal articles on AI, human–AI collaboration, employee creativity, innovative work behavior, algorithmic management, and innovation management. Building on established models of individual innovation, it develops a worker-centered framework linking four innovation stages with three higher-order AI functions: task execution, knowledge support, and organizational governance. The evidence is strongest for searching, idea generation, creativity, and short-term task performance, and remains limited for idea promotion, implementation, diffusion, and realized innovation outcomes. The synthesis identifies three central tensions: performance equalization versus capability differentiation, short-term quality versus long-term capability development, and individual improvement versus collective homogenization. AI can enhance innovation-related work through cognitive expansion, search acceleration, productivity release, recombination, feedback, and learning, but it can also reduce output diversity, weaken expertise development, intensify work, increase dependence, and shift managerial control over creative labor. The review positions AI as both a cognitive resource and an innovation-governance mechanism and outlines directions for future research on mechanisms, heterogeneity, novelty, capability accumulation, and responsible governance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Water Treatment and Quality Assessment
items.abstract: Measurement and regular monitoring of key water quality parameters, either in natural water bodies or in an engineered wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), are essential for assessing the overall system performance or identifying the root causes of water quality degradation. Advances in machine learning (ML) algorithms, remote sensing, and soft sensors have been transformative for water quality management programs. Satellite imagery and calibrated spectral indices can be used for long-term water quality monitoring or for a machine-learning-based water quality index. Data-driven ML models trained on historical data on influent characteristics, operating parameters, and labeled performance in municipal WWTPs can predict treatment efficiency and effluent quality. This chapter starts with an introduction to various ML model architectures, highlighting the stages in the model development exercise. The application of ML models in wastewater treatment and water quality prediction is discussed in subsequent sections. Finally, challenges and future perspectives in this domain are addressed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teacher Education: Pedagogical Innovations, Professional Competence, and Ethical Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing educational practices, creating new possibilities and challenges for teacher education. Its applications extend beyond automated content generation to lesson planning, instructional design, assessment, personalised learning, reflective practice, and professional development. These developments require teacher education institutions to reconsider how prospective and practising teachers acquire pedagogical knowledge, exercise professional judgement, and prepare learners for an AI-mediated educational environment. This article examines the implications of AI for teacher education through a thematic synthesis of published research and policy frameworks. The discussion is organised around five interconnected themes that examine the role of artificial intelligence in shaping the future of teacher education. These include the use of AI to support pedagogical innovation and improve instructional practices; the development of AI competence among prospective and practising teachers; the changing nature of assessment, feedback, and professional learning; the ethical, epistemological, and institutional challenges associated with AI adoption; and the strategies required to integrate AI responsibly into teacher education programmes. Together, these themes provide a basis for understanding how AI can enhance teaching and learning while addressing the professional, ethical, and institutional considerations necessary for its effective implementation. Research reviews indicate that AI can support instructional planning, feedback, resource development, and professional learning, although the strength and sustainability of these benefits depend on the design of learning activities and the preparation of teachers. Concerns relating to inaccurate outputs, algorithmic bias, privacy, academic integrity, unequal access, and overdependence on automated systems remain important. The article argues that active AI integration requires more than technical familiarity. Teacher education should develop the capacity to evaluate AI-generated information, design pedagogically appropriate learning experiences, protect learner interests, and retain human responsibility for educational decisions. It proposes a human-centred framework for integrating AI literacy, pedagogical competence, ethical judgement, reflective practice, and institutional support into teacher preparation. The article concludes that AI should strengthen teachers' professional capacity rather than diminish their agency, relationships with learners, or responsibility for educational quality.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE LAW
items.abstract: It is too early to definitively predict how generative artificial intelligence (‘AI’) will affect the law and the legal profession. How much of the hype will come to pass, or whether the effects of AI will be revolutionary or evolutionary is yet unknown. Although the extent of those effects may not be fully evident today, early glimpses show the potential for structural disruption is real, pervasive, and likely to be far-reaching. This paper explores four research questions, explored strategically in a contested internationally underdeveloped regulatory environment — with significant regulatory lag in Australia — amidst vast and rapid technological change. It posits that AI is not ‘intelligent’ of itself but that enterprises that deploy AI tools can then act intelligently. This objective requires updated enterprise governance frameworks. It also posits that potential convergence of AI and legal linguistics is a new scholarly field which could open the path to Artificial General Intelligence, a requirement for legal utility beyond prosaic applications. This paper develops the research questions into original contributions in modern enterprise governance and the necessary conjoining of AI and legal linguistics. It identifies a process of ‘enculturation’ as AI technology and legal stakeholders learn about each other globally. ‘Enculturation’ facilitates the ‘myriad moments’ — encountered in creative and artistic spirits implicit in negotiations and dealing with the unexpected in court. It establishes that future legal stakeholder utility is derived from the enhancement and/or replacement of sentient human intelligence rests upon the confluence of logic, plain language, and law, underpinned by a command of ethics, linguistics, legal linguistics and linguistics engineering. The paper then provides Digital Readiness guidance for legal stakeholders including directors, trustees, practitioners, arbitrators and judicial officers, and detailed proposals for the development of Australian law as means of reducing legal risks.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery—A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly growing in the field of dental medicine and in oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMS). The aim of the present review is to assess current applications of AI in OMS, to evaluate their advantages and limitations, and to identify areas requiring further research. Materials and Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with targeted keywords including “artificial intelligence,” “deep learning,” “machine learning,” “oral surgery,” “maxillofacial surgery,” and “diagnosis “Artificial Intelligence” OR “Machine Learning” OR “Deep Learning” AND “Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery” OR “Oral Surgery” OR “Maxillofacial Surgery” AND “Diagnosis”. Of 308 identified studies, 37 met the inclusion criteria focusing on AI-assisted detection interpretation and surgical planning in OMS. Results: AI is effective in identifying anatomical landmarks, evaluating lesions and cysts, diagnosing bone disease like medication-related osteonecrosis of jaws (MRONJ), planning dental implants, and aiding in the classification of fractures and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders. AI can match or outperform human experts in various diagnostic tasks, particularly in panoramic and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) image analysis. AI shows promise in early detection of impacted and supernumerary teeth, maxillofacial pathologies, neoplastic conditions, and soft tissue calcifications. Limitations: However, substantial methodological heterogeneity, inconsistent reporting of AI performance metrics, and limited external validation across the included studies constrain direct comparison of results and assessment of the generalizability of reported AI performance. Conclusions: AI may assist clinicians in diagnostic and treatment-related decision-making, but current evidence does not support its use as a replacement for comprehensive clinical assessment and professional judgment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Pediatric Primary Care for Weight Management: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric overweight and obesity (OW/OB) is a major public health concern associated with significant short- and long-term health risks. Primary care is a key setting for early identification and management, yet current approaches face barriers related to implementation, workflow, and family engagement. This systematic review examined how artificial intelligence (AI) has been used in pediatric primary care and closely connected clinical settings to support OW/OB management. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251103662) and reported according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL Ultimate, Compendex, and CENTRAL were searched for English-language studies published from 2007 to July 9, 2025. Eligible studies included children and adolescents ages 5-19 years with OW/OB, were conducted in or linked to primary care, and included at least one AI-based approach. Dual-reviewer screening, structured data extraction, and methodological appraisal using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool were completed. RESULTS: Of 3854 records identified, 20 studies met inclusion criteria. Most studies (80%) targeted patient families, while 20% included both families and clinicians. Machine learning was the most common AI approach (60%) and was primarily used for obesity risk prediction or stratification. Fewer studies examined family engagement, counseling, documentation review, or generative AI tools. Methodological quality ranged from moderate to high. DISCUSSION: AI tools in pediatric primary care primarily support early identification of OW/OB risk, but evidence on workflow integration, sustained engagement, and long-term clinical impact remains limited. Future research should prioritize prospective, workflow-embedded studies, meaningful clinical outcomes, equity, privacy, governance, clinician training, and policy oversight.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Enhancing Safety Measures and User Satisfaction in Federal University Libraries in North-East Nigeria: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies influencing library operations and information service delivery across the globe. The increasing complexity of security threats, technological advancement, and users' expectations has necessitated the adoption of intelligent systems capable of improving safety management and enhancing user satisfaction in academic libraries. Federal university libraries in North-East Nigeria are expected to provide safe, secure, technology-driven, and user-centred learning environments that support teaching, learning, research, and innovation. However, inadequate technological infrastructure, poor funding, limited AI adoption, insufficient digital competencies among library personnel, cybersecurity threats, and weak institutional support continue to hinder effective safety management and quality service delivery. This paper conceptually examines Artificial Intelligence as a catalyst for enhancing safety measures and user satisfaction in federal university libraries in North-East Nigeria. Specifically, the paper discusses the concepts of Artificial Intelligence, safety measures, user satisfaction, and academic libraries; examines relevant theoretical perspectives; identifies challenges affecting AI adoption; and proposes strategies for integrating AI into library safety management. The paper adopts a conceptual review methodology through the analysis of current scholarly literature. It concludes that AI technologies such as intelligent surveillance systems, biometric access control, predictive analytics, chatbots, smart sensors, facial recognition technologies, and machine learning applications possess significant potential for improving library safety, operational efficiency, and users' satisfaction. The paper recommends increased investment in AI infrastructure, continuous staff capacity building, supportive institutional policies, and strategic partnerships to facilitate sustainable AI integration in federal university libraries.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence based chatbot for solar panels quality assurance
items.abstract: The paper addresses the need for improved solar panel quality assurance by developing an AI-based chatbot system tailored for installers and manufacturers. Traditional quality assurance is often slow, resource-intensive, and subject to human error. Leveraging advances in large language models, the chatbot provides automated support for performance testing, failure detection, and maintenance guidance. Implemented using Promptly and Flowise AI platforms, the system incorporates domain-specific knowledge through Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It delivers technical recommendations, identifies frequent failure points, and offers actionable advice to enhance diagnostic efficiency and maintenance effectiveness. Performance comparisons between platforms show distinct operational characteristics, underscoring the impact of system choice on user experience. Overall, the chatbot demonstrates promising potential to streamline solar panel testing, maintenance, and decision-making processes for industry professionals.
