items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Benign Esophageal Stricture Dilation: An Evidence‐Transferability Framework and Safety‐First Roadmap
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Endoscopic dilation is first‐line therapy for symptomatic benign esophageal strictures but remains operator‐dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) could support assessment, risk stratification, and documentation; however, evidence from adjacent tasks is often mistaken for procedure‐specific validation. Aim To map the evidence for AI in benign esophageal stricture dilation, assess transferability and methodological quality, and propose a translational pathway. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Europe PMC from inception through June 28, 2026, using prespecified searches in adults and children. Studies were classified by evidence provenance and appraised using design‐adapted domain considerations. Results Within the search date and eligibility criteria, no AI system was identified that guided, monitored, or assessed dilation itself; two retrospective single‐center studies applied machine learning in the target population for other tasks. Adjacent neoplasia and engineering studies support component feasibility, while clinical cohorts identify candidate predictors. Functional lumen imaging probe technology provides non‐AI measurement and potential reference labels. Recurrent concerns included selected or retrospective samples, limited external validation, and high concern about applicability to dilation. Performance cannot be transferred across mismatched target tasks, acquisition physics, reference standards, populations or operating contexts, or consequences of error. Conclusion Adjacent evidence can justify candidate components. Procedure‐specific calibration and validation remain necessary. Priorities are calibrated morphometric variables with prespecified reference standards and reproducible documentation using synchronized multimodal and outcome data. External validation should be followed by human‐controlled advisory testing before intraprocedural automation.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR FEATURE RECOGNITION AND LI-RADS CLASSIFICATION ON COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY AND MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF DIAGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE AND EXTERNAL VALIDATION
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence may reduce variability and workload in computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging assessment of liver observations, but high internal performance does not establish transportability or clinical benefit. This systematic review evaluates artificial-intelligence methods explicitly linked to Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System feature recognition, category assignment, or category-informed diagnosis, with emphasis on diagnostic performance and external validation. PubMed was searched through October 3, 2026 using prespecified LI-RADS, artificial-intelligence, and cross-sectional-imaging concepts. Seventy-three records were identified and eighteen original studies met the operational eligibility criteria. Evidence included radiomics, conventional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transformer architectures, self-configuring segmentation systems, post hoc explainability methods, and a report-based large language model. Performance was not directly poolable because studies addressed different targets: arterial-phase hyperenhancement, washout, enhancing capsule, ancillary features, LR-3 versus LR-4/5 discrimination, multicategory grading, LR-M subtyping, lesion detection, or hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis. Several internal studies reported high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve or classification accuracy, but the strongest direct category-classification pilot fell from 60.4% internal accuracy to 41.2% and 47.7% in external computed-tomography and magnetic-resonance-imaging cohorts. A stepwise magnetic-resonance-imaging system also demonstrated external degradation for individual major features, particularly washout and capsule, despite relatively stable category accuracy. More recent multicenter studies showed improved robustness and clinically meaningful reader assistance, but true site-independent validation, calibration, prospective impact analysis, subgroup fairness, and failure-mode reporting remained uncommon. Feature-guided systems were generally more interpretable than end-to-end category predictors, while report-based language models answered a different question from image-level recognition. The available evidence supports AI as an adjunct for standardized feature assessment and reader support, not autonomous replacement of LI-RADS interpretation. Clinical readiness requires independent multivendor validation, pathology or rigorous longitudinal reference standards appropriate to the target, locked algorithms, calibrated outputs, human–AI workflow evaluation, and transparent reporting of exclusions, indeterminate cases, and domain shift.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Ovarian Health Assessment: A Survey of Ultrasound, Multimodal Learning, Explainable AI and Longitudinal Approaches
items.abstract: Evaluating the health of ovaries demands corroboration across symptoms, menstrual and reproductive history, lab values, ultrasound imagery, and prior clinical encounters. We review recent artificial-intelligence work surrounding ovarian health across ultrasound analysis, clinical natural- language processing, multimodal learning, explainable AI, uncertainty estimation, and longitudinal modelling. Our work included researching recent indexed, peerreviewed literature with targeted searches, screening the results, and analyzing two datasets based on modality, task, algorithm, dataset attributes, validation strategies, explainability, and temporal modelling. Current literature is advancing rapidly in image-based and multimodal ovarian diagnosis but also exhibits several key consistent limitations including retrospective datasets with little to no external validation, heterogeneous labels, incomplete patient-level multimodal pairings, and reliance on cross-sectional prediction. Although the volume of longitudinal-specific ovarian AI is sparse in comparison, recent research illustrates that longitudinal modelling can be done explicitly. Through our analysis we identify an opportunity for a connected, doctor-facing system that leverages clinical text, sonography reports and ultrasound images, other medical or lab reports, visit-level structured evidence, and patient-level longitudinal reasoning. From here we motivate OvaCare, whose output for each encounter can be broken down into two parts: OUTPUT 1, a structured clinical insight contributed to a patient timeline, and OUTPUT 2, a longitudinal clinical insight generated from analyzing subsequent visits. Ultimately, the end result of this review is not only a current summary of work in ovarian-focused AI, but also provides research-gapdriven justification for OvaCare 's multimodal and temporal methodologies.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ACCOUNTING AND AUDITING: TRANSFORMING FINANCIAL DECISION-MAKING AND PROFESSIONAL PRACTICES
items.abstract: Abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed accounting and auditing practices across organizations worldwide. The increasing availability of financial data, advancements in machine learning algorithms, and the demand for real-time financial information have accelerated the adoption of AI-driven technologies in accounting and auditing functions. Traditional accounting systems primarily relied on manual data processing and periodic reporting, whereas AI enables continuous monitoring, predictive analytics, automated transaction processing, and intelligent decision support. In auditing, AI enhances fraud detection, risk assessment, anomaly identification, and audit quality through automated analysis of large volumes of structured and unstructured financial data. The integration of technologies such as Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Robotic Process Automation (RPA), and Generative AI has redefined professional roles and transformed the manner in which financial information is generated, analyzed, and interpreted. Despite numerous benefits, the adoption of AI also raises concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, ethical accountability, and workforce readiness. This paper examines the role of AI in accounting and auditing, explores its influence on financial decision-making, evaluates its benefits and challenges, and discusses future implications for accounting professionals. The study is conceptual in nature and is based on an extensive review of recent academic literature and professional reports. The findings indicate that AI acts as an enabler of enhanced efficiency, accuracy, and strategic decision-making while complementing rather than replacing human expertise in accounting and auditing.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in central nervous system autoimmune diseases: from clinical decision support to mechanistic discovery and translation
items.abstract: Abstract Central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), autoimmune encephalitis (AE), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), remain difficult to diagnose, stratify, and treat because clinical phenotypes overlap, biomarkers are imperfect, and the disease course requires longitudinal observation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being evaluated to integrate clinical, imaging, immunological, and molecular data for decision-making in neuroimmunology. Clinical applications include automated neuroimaging analysis, differential diagnosis, disease classification, relapse prediction, prognostic stratification, and risk-informed care planning. Evidence is unevenly distributed: MS has the largest body of published work, particularly in neuroimaging, whereas studies in NMOSD, AE, and MOGAD are smaller, more heterogeneous, and often lack external validation. Computational approaches are also being applied to multi-omics, single-cell and spatial data, molecular target prioritisation, drug repositioning, trial enrichment, digital biomarkers, federated learning, and longitudinal modelling; however, these applications generally provide association, prioritisation, or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than validated therapeutic benefit. This Review maps reported applications, evidence patterns, and methodological and implementation needs rather than ranking translational maturity or implying established clinical benefit.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Construction Delay Analysis and Management: A Review
items.abstract: Introduction Construction delays remain a challenge in projects, often resulting in cost overruns, disputes, productivity losses, and schedule inefficiencies. Growing project complexity has increased the need for data-driven approaches to delay analysis and management. This study reviews the application of artificial intelligence in construction delay analysis and management by examining application areas, techniques, project contexts, implementation maturity, and research gaps. Methods A structured literature review was conducted using a PRISMA-guided search and screening process. Scopus and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following database filtering, title and abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment, 42 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. Results The reviewed studies applied artificial intelligence to delay prediction, delay-cause identification, risk prioritisation, progress monitoring, schedule recovery, and optimisation using machine learning, deep learning, ensemble learning, and hybrid modelling approaches. Several studies reported predictive accuracy above 90%, particularly for artificial neural networks, ensemble techniques, and hybrid optimisation models. However, evidence remains constrained by limited datasets, project-specific applications, weak real-time data integration, and insufficient consideration of contractual and external factors. Discussion The reviewed studies indicate that Artificial Intelligence (AI) models have improved predictive capability in construction delay management. However, practical implementation remains limited by data availability, model interpretability, and weak integration with project decision-making processes. Conclusion Artificial intelligence can improve construction delay management through transparent and data-driven approaches. Further research is needed to develop integrated frameworks linking predictive analytics with practical delay-management decisions in dynamic construction environments.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in criminal investigation: effects of large language model consultation on confirmation bias in a simulated investigation game
items.abstract: Objectives Confirmation bias can distort information search and evidence interpretation in criminal investigations. We tested whether consulting a large language model (LLM) could reduce this bias in group decisions.Methods In total, 108 participants formed 36 three-person teams randomly assigned to LLM consultation, theory-based information and debiasing strategies, or unaided control. Teams investigated homicide cases adapted from real cases in a web-based game. Outcomes were investigative cues opened, deliberation time, and culpability assigned to true perpetrators versus innocent suspects.Results Group assignment had no main effect on overall culpability accuracy or deliberation time. In weighted analyses, group interacted with case type: controls were less accurate in wrongful – than correct-conviction cases, whereas this difference was numerically smaller in the LLM and theory groups. The interaction was nonsignificant in unweighted analyses and should be interpreted cautiously. The LLM group opened more cues than controls in wrongful-conviction cases.Conclusions LLM consultation increased information search in wrongful-conviction cases but did not clearly improve accuracy. Theory-based support showed a numerically smaller weighted accuracy penalty, but no clear advantage of LLM consultation over theory-based support was established. These findings inform the design of AI-assisted investigative decision support.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies in modern healthcare and is increasingly influencing contemporary dental practice.Recent advancements in machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and generative AI have enabled the development of intelligent systems capable of analyzing complex clinical, radiographic, and histopathological datasets with remarkable precision.AI applications have demonstrated substantial benefits across multiple dental specialties, including oral radiology, oral pathology, orthodontics, periodontology, prosthodontics, conservative dentistry and endodontics, oral and maxillofacial surgery, pediatric dentistry, and public health dentistry.These technologies facilitate early disease detection, automated image interpretation, treatment planning, outcome prediction, and workflow optimization.The integration of AI with digital dentistry technologies such as cone-beam computed tomography, intraoral scanners, computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing systems, and electronic health records has accelerated its adoption in clinical settings.Despite these advantages, challenges such as data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, transparency issues, implementation costs, and regulatory uncertainties continue to limit widespread clinical implementation.Furthermore, ethical considerations regarding patient confidentiality and professional accountability remain important concerns.This review provides a comprehensive overview of current AI applications in dentistry, recent technological advancements, existing limitations, and future opportunities for integrating AI into routine dental practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Economic and Financial Communication: Challenges, Practices, and Perspectives for More Transparent and Efficient Information
items.abstract: In a context of accelerated digital transformation, this article examines the extent to which and the conditions under which artificial intelligence (AI) transforms economic and financial communication by improving information quality, transparency, and decision-making efficiency. Drawing on agency theory, information asymmetry, and information governance, it proposes a conceptual model articulating a chain of relationships whereby AI influences information quality, which in turn shapes transparency, ultimately improving decision-making performance, while also integrating a direct effect of AI on that performance and a risk of algorithmic opacity. The model further incorporates moderating variables: information governance arrangements, data quality, and the complementarity between human expertise and intelligent systems, resulting in eight research hypotheses covering both direct and moderating effects across the model. An exploratory qualitative study, based on semi-structured interviews with twenty-three professionals from the public and private sectors, conducted either in person or remotely and processed through thematic analysis, shows that AI is predominantly perceived as a lever for automation, reliability, and decision support, particularly through the reduction of human errors and the processing of massive data volumes. However, these effects remain conditional upon the quality of input data, adequate governance arrangements, and the maintenance of human oversight, while risks of algorithmic opacity, bias, hallucinations, and confidentiality persist, alongside a structural lag in adoption within the public sector. The article therefore supports a contingent, non-techno-deterministic understanding of AI in economic and financial communication, in which technological value added remains subordinate to data quality, governance, and human intervention rather than to the technology itself.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in English Language Learning: Student Perspectives on AI Literacy, Academic Integrity, and Dependency at Universidad Tecnológica de Tijuana
items.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created new opportunities for English language learning while also raising concerns regarding academic integrity, student dependency, AI literacy, and institutional regulation. This study aims to analyze university students’ perceptions of these four dimensions in the context of English language learning at a technological university in Mexico. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and correlational research design was employed. Data were collected from 214 university students through a 16-item questionnaire organized into four constructs: Academic Integrity, AI Literacy, AI Dependency, and Institutional Regulation. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson’s correlation coefficient, and Kruskal–Wallis tests were used to analyze the data. The results showed relatively high levels of AI Literacy (M = 3.77, SD = 0.88) and Academic Integrity (M = 3.61, SD = 0.86), whereas AI Dependency obtained a lower mean (M = 2.61, SD = 0.78). AI Literacy was positively correlated with Academic Integrity (r = .684, p < .001), while Academic Integrity and AI Literacy were also positively associated with Institutional Regulation. AI Dependency showed weak negative correlations with Academic Integrity and AI Literacy. Significant differences according to frequency of AI use were found for AI Dependency and Institutional Regulation, but not for Academic Integrity or AI Literacy. The findings suggest that responsible AI integration in English language education requires more than regulating access to technology; it also requires developing students’ AI literacy, maintaining academic integrity, and promoting learner autonomy through clear institutional guidance.

items.abstract: Functional gastrointestinal disorders, now termed disorders of gut-brain interaction, are heterogeneous conditions shaped by psychological, physiological, microbial, and environmental factors.Diagnosis and treatment remain difficult because symptoms overlap, trajectories fluctuate, and no single objective biomarker exists.This minireview synthesises human evidence for artificial intelligence (AI) in symptom classification, digital phenotyping, microbiome and multi-omics prediction, treatment-response estimation, wearable monitoring, and language-based care.Targeted PubMed searches were updated through September 20, 2026.Current studies show feasibility, but most use small, single-centre cohorts, retrospective designs, or internal validation; calibration and prospective impact evaluation are uncommon.The most plausible near-term role of AI is therefore clinical augmentation: Identifying longitudinal patterns, supporting shared decisions, and detecting changes that require reassessment while preserving human oversight and patient autonomy.Large language models may improve education and communication, but disorder-specific evaluations reveal imperfect diagnosis and treatment recommendations with marked overconfidence.Translation requires representative cohorts that include overlapping organic disease, explicit endpoints despite the absence of a diagnostic gold standard, external validation, calibration, equity assessment, and prospective evaluation of patient benefit.AI should be judged by outcomes and care experience, not discrimination alone.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education From Automation to Responsible Augmentation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often presented as a sequence of increasingly capable tools, yet educational outcomes do not rise automatically with model capability. This narrative review argues that the decisive variable is alignment: AI produces durable educational value when its affordances are aligned with pedagogy, assessment, educator agency, and institutional governance. The review traces the field from automation and learning analytics through adaptive support and generative co-production to an emerging model of responsible augmentation. Recent meta-analyses, controlled studies, systematic reviews, policy documents, and selected empirical studies were critically compared across three interdependent domains: resources and learning environments; teaching and learning; and management, assessment, and evaluation. The synthesis explains why apparently contradictory findings coexist. Structured, curriculum-aligned AI tutoring can improve immediate learning, whereas unconstrained answer generation can raise supported performance while weakening independent performance. Likewise, automated assessment can improve feedback speed but becomes educationally unsafe when opaque scores or unreliable detectors are treated as final decisions. Evidence concerning international and multilingual learners further shows that language, culture, affect, and data representation are not peripheral variables. The review proposes a responsible-augmentation framework in which alignment, agency, equity, and accountability operate across all three domains. It concludes with a research agenda prioritising longitudinal transfer, calibrated human–AI collaboration, subgroup validity, transparent governance, and institution-level implementation studies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education—Ethical Policies Mapping
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is transforming numerous sectors, and education is no exception. The adoption of generative AI tools in higher education presents significant opportunities for enhancing teaching, learning, assessment, accessibility, and administrative processes. At the same time, their widespread use raises critical ethical concerns related to academic integrity, bias, transparency, data protection, and the possible erosion of critical thinking and creativity. In response, higher education institutions worldwide are beginning to formulate ethical guidelines to govern the use of AI by students, educators, and administrators. However, institutional responses remain diverse across different contexts. This study examines how academic institutions across different countries conceptualise ethical AI use, define risks, and operationalise principles in practical policies through mapping 55 higher education institutions, complemented by an extended analysis of 87 documents. Across the six analysed thematic categories, transparency and disclosure, academic integrity, data protection and privacy, accountability, and risk mitigation are more consistently addressed than accessibility and inclusion. The analysis identifies practical guidance and recognised legitimate AI uses. The discussion considers the interpretation of AI and recommends aligning its use with ethical standards. The article concludes with a summary of the results and directions for future research.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT: IMPLICATIONS FOR HUMAN CAPITAL AND THE FUTURE WORKFORCE
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming Human Resource Management (HRM) by changing the way organizations recruit, develop, evaluate and retain employees. AI-enabled technologies are being applied across several HR functions, including talent acquisition, workforce planning, performance evaluation, employee development and compensation. While these technologies offer opportunities for improved efficiency, data-driven decision-making and personalized employee services, their use also raises important concerns regarding bias, privacy, transparency, fairness and the role of human judgement. This paper examines the implications of Artificial Intelligence for Human Resource Management, with particular emphasis on human capital development and the future workforce. The paper argues that AI should be viewed primarily as a tool for augmenting human capabilities rather than simply replacing employees. Organizations must therefore invest in employee reskilling, digital capability development and responsible AI governance. The study concludes that the future effectiveness of HRM will depend on the ability of organizations to combine technological innovation with ethical principles and human-centred management practices. The study emphasizes that AI adoption is not only a technological issue but also a human capital and workforce-development challenge.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in mathematics education: a systematic review of pedagogical impact, cognitive outcomes, and ethical implications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping mathematics education, yet reviews remain fragmented by tool, level, or outcome. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC (2015–2025) and included 46 of 4,475 records, all published from 2022 onward and appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (κ = 0.762). Generative AI accounted for half of the studies. AI use was associated mainly with procedural, engagement, and self-regulation gains, whereas support for deep reasoning and proof remained fragile. Teachers acted as designers, supervisors, co-creators, and AI literacy mentors; ethical risks included hallucination, academic integrity, over-reliance, and a Global South gap. We propose a Pedagogical–Cognitive–Ethical (PCE) framework in which teachers mediate these interdependent dimensions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Criminal Forensics in India: Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the field of criminal forensics in India by enhancing the efficiency, speed and accuracy of criminal investigations. AI-powered technologies such as facial recognition systems, predictive analytics, biometric identification, digital surveillance and machine learning algorithms are increasingly being used by investigative agencies to analyse evidence, identify suspects and detect criminal patterns. In the context of rising cybercrimes, organized crimes and digital offences, AI has emerged as a significant tool for modernizing forensic science and strengthening the criminal justice system. Despite its advantages, the use of AI in criminal forensics also raises several legal, ethical and constitutional concerns. Issues relating to privacy, data protection, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency and reliability of AI-generated evidence pose serious challenges to the Indian legal framework. The absence of comprehensive legislation regulating AI usage in criminal investigations further creates uncertainty regarding accountability and admissibility of AI-based evidence in courts. Additionally, overdependence on automated systems may threaten fundamental rights and procedural fairness if proper safeguards are not implemented. This paper critically examines the opportunities and challenges associated with the application of AI in modern criminal forensics in India. It explores the technological advancements, their impact on forensic investigations and the need for a balanced legal and regulatory framework that ensures both effective crime detection and protection of individual rights in a society.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Clinical Decision-Making: A Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: This project is a scoping review entitled "Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Clinical Decision-Making." It maps the scientific evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) tools that pharmacists use to support clinical decision-making in pharmaceutical services. AI is increasingly used in healthcare for diagnosis, prognosis and clinical decision support. In pharmacy, it has potential in prescription analysis, drug interaction screening, dose adjustment and adverse event monitoring. However, its use in pharmacy practice is still incipient and mostly oriented toward operational tasks such as inventory management and process optimization. Evidence on the direct clinical use of AI by pharmacists, and on its effects on patient safety and clinical outcomes, remains scarce and dispersed. A scoping review suits this emerging, heterogeneous field, where there is not yet enough homogeneous evidence for a synthesis of effectiveness. The review is part of the project SisAPEC Farma, aims to develop AI tools to support pharmaceutical clinical decision-making. The review will therefore provide the scientific grounding for the system's pharmaceutical module. Objective The primary objective is to map the scientific evidence on the use of AI-based tools employed by pharmacists to support clinical decision-making in pharmaceutical services, in Brazil or in other countries. The research question follows the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework: Population: pharmacists involved in clinical services or direct patient care. Concept: the use, development, evaluation or implementation of AI-based tools or systems to support clinical decision-making. Context: clinical services provided by pharmacists in different practice settings (primary care, community pharmacies, hospitals, outpatient services and clinics). Methods The review follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, which builds on the Arksey and O'Malley framework. The protocol was written using the guidance and template of Lely et al. (2023), and the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) will guide reporting. Eligibility: The review will include studies involving pharmacists working in clinical services or direct patient care. These studies must describe, develop, evaluate or implement AI tools (machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, generative AI, expert systems and AI-based clinical decision support systems) applied to clinical pharmacy practice. Studies with peripheral pharmacist involvement will be excluded, as will studies focused exclusively on non-clinical activities (administrative management, logistics, inventory, dispensing automation) and studies on industrial or drug-discovery applications with no clinical pharmacy use. Only records with available full text will be included. No language or date limits will be applied. Search strategy: The strategy was developed for MEDLINE/PubMed and adapted to Embase, the Virtual Health Library (BVS), Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library. Grey literature (Google Scholar, ProQuest and OpenGrey), hand-searching of reference lists and expert consultation will complement it. Controlled vocabularies (MeSH, DeCS, Emtree) and free-text terms will be combined. Because Population and Context cover the same conceptual universe (pharmacists and the clinical pharmacy services in which they work), they are combined with OR, and this block is then combined with the AI concept block using AND. Selection and charting: Records will be deduplicated in EndNote 20 and screened in Rayyan by two independent, blinded reviewers in two stages (title/abstract, then full text). Disagreements will be resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer, and reasons for exclusion at full-text stage will be recorded. Data will be charted independently by two reviewers using a piloted Excel form adapted from JBI SUMARI. It will cover study identification, context and population, AI tool characteristics, results, barriers and facilitators, and gaps and opportunities. Synthesis: Analysis will be descriptive, using absolute and relative frequencies. Where pertinent, basic qualitative content analysis will combine an inductive and a deductive step. Results will be presented in tables, figures, narrative summaries and a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. Any AI-based automation used to support the review will operate only under supervision, with all decisions validated by human reviewers. Expected Results The review is expected to produce a comprehensive map of the nature and extent of the evidence on AI tools used by pharmacists for clinical decision-making, including the types of tools, their functionalities and the clinical processes they support; a characterization of the available evidence on usability, acceptability, feasibility, performance, implementation and clinical impact, showing where evidence is concentrated and where it is lacking; an identification of the practice settings and countries in which these technologies have been most studied. A systematized overview of the technical, ethical, regulatory and organizational barriers and facilitators to implementing AI in clinical pharmacy; a clear identification of research gaps and unmet needs, pointing to opportunities for developing or improving AI solutions aligned with real clinical pharmacy needs and; by clarifying what is known and what is still missing, the review is expected to advance the field. It will support the safe, evidence-based development and implementation of AI in clinical pharmacy, including the pharmaceutical module of SisAPEC Farma. It will also inform future research, practice and policy.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Readiness Among Nursing Students: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: This scoping review aims to systematically map and synthesize the existing literature on artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and readiness among nursing students in educational and clinical learning contexts. The review will examine how AI literacy and readiness are conceptualized, defined, and measured among nursing students. It will identify the levels and dimensions of AI-related knowledge, skills, competencies, attitudes, confidence, and preparedness reported in the literature, as well as factors associated with students' readiness to engage with AI technologies in nursing education and future professional practice. The review will also explore the educational strategies, training initiatives, assessment instruments, and institutional factors discussed in relation to the development of AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The review will be guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Relevant evidence from quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies will be considered, subject to predefined eligibility criteria. A systematic search of relevant bibliographic databases and supplementary sources will be undertaken, followed by transparent study selection, data charting, and descriptive and thematic mapping of the available evidence. Findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), where applicable. The anticipated outcome is a comprehensive overview of the scope, characteristics, measurement approaches, educational applications, and research gaps relating to AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The findings may inform future research, nursing curricula, AI-related educational interventions, and the development of relevant competencies and assessment frameworks.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy in social research: A bibliometric analysis of conceptual evolution and emerging trends
items.abstract: In contemporary digital society, artificial intelligence literacy (AI literacy) has become a key competence that enables citizens to understand and actively participate in increasingly automated environments. However, despite the rapid growth of scientific output, partly driven by tools such as ChatGPT, the literature reveals substantial conceptual fragmentation that hinders an integrated understanding of its educational and ethical dimensions. In this context, this study aimed to analyze the intellectual evolution and conceptual structure of research on AI literacy, based on Scopus-indexed literature. A bibliometric methodology was applied to a corpus of 2,645 documents using scientific mapping techniques to identify publication patterns, collaboration networks, and dominant thematic streams. The results reveal an accelerated expansion of the field and a shift from early approaches focused primarily on educational contexts such as K-12 education and computational thinking toward more complex frameworks that incorporate algorithmic ethics, psychological acceptance of technology, critical thinking, and academic integrity challenges associated with generative AI (GenAI). Overall, this study contributes to the educational technology literature by providing a longitudinal bibliometric interpretation of the evolution of AI literacy and by identifying emerging research agendas related to GenAI, ethical reasoning, and critical digital competencies in contemporary education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Marketing dan Consumer Trust sebagai Determinan Purchase Intention Generasi Z
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the influence of Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Consumer Trust on Purchase Intention in Generation Z consumers. A sample of 100 Generation Z respondents who actively use digital media and are exposed to AI-based marketing was selected using purposive sampling techniques. Data were collected through a Likert scale questionnaire of 1–5 and analyzed using multiple linear regression, t-test, F test, and determination coefficient (R2) test. The results showed that partially, Artificial Intelligence Marketing (t = 12.021; p = 0.000) and Consumer Trust (t = 7.873; p = 0.000) had a positive and significant effect on Purchase Intent. Simultaneously, Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Consumer Trust had a significant effect on Purchase Intention (F = 278.811; p = 0.000). A determination coefficient value (R2) of 0.852 showed that 85.2% of the variation in Purchase Intention was influenced by these two variables, while the remaining 14.8% was influenced by other factors outside the model. This study concludes that optimizing personalization-based AI marketing strategies coupled with maintaining consumer trust is a key determinant in encouraging Generation Z's buying interest.

items.title: Artificial intelligence transparency statements and publication governance in medical literature: cross-sectional analysis of 97,916 articles, 2015–2026
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across scholarly writing, peer review, and editorial workflows, creating new research integrity questions about attribution, accountability, and disclosure. We measured how explicit artificial intelligence (AI) transparency statements are appearing in published medical literature and whether scalable full-text methods can monitor their adoption across journals and specialties. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of 97,916 English-language medical journal articles published from 2015 through April 2026 across 14 medical and surgical fields. Full text was retrieved from PubMed Central XML or publisher-hosted article files and classified with a large language model for positive AI-use disclosure, explicit statements of non-use, named tools, use cases, and statement location. Validation used pre-ChatGPT specificity, second-model agreement in 10,979 articles, and blinded human review of 300 stratified cases by 2 independent reviewers with adjudication. All rates were recalculated excluding Frontiers journals, whose submission workflow applies a standardized AI declaration. Any AI transparency statement increased from 1.4% in 2023 to 22.4% in January-April 2026, or 9.9% excluding Frontiers journals. Positive disclosure reached 7.3% (6.2% excluding Frontiers), while negative disclosure reached 15.1% (3.7% excluding Frontiers). Frontiers contributed 6.1% of articles but 71.1% of negative disclosures. Health Informatics and Digital Medicine had the highest positive disclosure rate during 2023–2026 (11.1%; 10.5% excluding Frontiers). Among 91 journals with at least 20 classified articles in 2025–2026, statement rates ranged from 0 to 100%, and all 3 journals at 100% were Frontiers titles. Language refinement was the most common disclosed use (72.8%). Inter-model agreement was high (Cohen kappa = 0.96 positive, 0.98 negative), and blinded human review confirmed 93.3% and 97.3% of these classifications, respectively. AI transparency statements are becoming a measurable publication-governance signal, but their prevalence is driven substantially by publisher submission infrastructure rather than author initiative: one publisher accounted for 71.1% of all negative disclosures. Near-universal declaration capture is therefore achievable through workflow design, and low observed disclosure rates may reflect missing declaration fields more than author reticence. Scalable full-text monitoring may help editors, publishers, and research integrity stakeholders evaluate policy implementation and distinguish assistive from generative AI use.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted spatial correction of augmented reality projections; implementing radiation mapping during radioguided robotic surgery
items.abstract: Abstract Translation of the drop-in gamma probe transformed radioguided robot-assisted prostate cancer (PCa) surgery. This study evaluated whether digitization of radiometric signals could allow conversion into more easier to interpret Augmented Reality radiation mapping (AR RM ) displays. 20 PCa patients were included who underwent robot-assisted sentinel node (SN)- and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) radioguided resections (24 SNs, 16 PSMA-avid nodes and 1 PSMA-avid primary tumor). Radiometric probe counts/s (dimensionless) synchronized with positional probe data allowed the retrospective creation of dynamic AR RM overlays in two dimensions. Artificial intelligence was used to segment out, and automatically track, surgical instruments and dynamically de-occlude the AR RM displays accordingly. Retrospective scoring by end-users indicated a 72.5% preference for the AR RM displays compared to the currently available radiometric display (bipolar scale; median ≥2; p < 0.001). Thus, indicating that video-feed embedded AR RM visualizations provide a digital means to further advance the surgeon’s perception of intraoperative molecular imaging.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted surrogate networks for thermal energy transport in radiative nanofluid model containing oxytactic microorganisms with mass flux-free conditions
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the thermal energy transfer in radiative nanofluid flow of oxytactic microorganisms under zero mass flux conditions with potential application in engineering systems. The investigation concerns free convection over an isothermal perpendicular cone in a permeable medium filled with a nanofluid. Design/methodology/approach A deep learning-based nonlinear autoregressive exogenous neural network optimized with Levenberg–Marquardt backpropagation (NARX-DNN-LMBP) is designed for the model of the radiative nanofluidic flow with microorganism (RNF-MO). It includes the effects of Brownian motion, solar radiation, thermophoresis, convective heating, suspended nanoparticles and oxytactic microorganisms along with zero mass flux boundary conditions. The synthetic data set is created using the Lobatto IIIA numerical solver and then randomly split into training, validation and test sets used to develop the neural network. Findings The proposed NARX-DNN-LMBP approach is found to be effective in predicting the RNF-MO model for various physical scenarios with mean squared error as low as 10−10. It is further evaluated with the mean squared error convergence trends, error histograms and error autocorrelation analysis to show accurate and reliable computational performance. Originality/value The novelty is achieved by coupling the NARX-DNN-LMBP deep learning framework with the Lobatto IIIA solver for fluid flow of complex radiative nanofluid with oxytactic microorganisms under zero mass flux condition. By simultaneously considering Brownian motion, convective heating, solar radiation and thermophoresis, a comprehensive computational framework for advanced thermal transport analysis can be provided.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven design of smart biomaterials for next-generation tissue engineering and personalized regeneration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in tissue engineering as a data-driven tool for linking biomaterial composition, scaffold architecture, fabrication parameters, and biological responses. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches have been applied to predict scaffold properties such as mechanical behavior, porosity, and degradation, and to support biomaterial selection and optimization of biofabrication parameters, including extrusion pressure, printing speed, and material formulation. AI-assisted imaging and sensing can also support in-line monitoring of printing quality and provide a basis for emerging feedback-enabled and adaptive biofabrication strategies. Beyond fabrication, data-driven and hybrid computational models are being investigated for analysis of cell–material interactions and tissue microenvironments, including spatial, mechanical, and transport-related phenomena. AI-assisted approaches have also been applied to nanocarrier formulation and drug-release prediction, where physicochemical and environmental variables can be integrated to support formulation design and forecast release behavior. Emerging digital-twin frameworks extend these concepts by combining patient-specific imaging, computational modeling, and AI-assisted design to support individualized scaffold development. However, most current applications remain computational, retrospective, in vitro, or preclinical, and high predictive performance does not necessarily indicate translational readiness. Limited and heterogeneous datasets, insufficient external validation, fabrication constraints, bioink rheology, crosslinking variability, cell viability, model interpretability, and regulatory requirements continue to limit reproducibility and clinical translation. This review therefore provides a pragmatic, application-oriented assessment of AI in tissue engineering, emphasizing demonstrated capabilities, current validation levels, and the remaining gap between computational prediction and reproducible, clinically relevant biofabrication.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Smart Home Systems: Technologies, Applications and Future Challenges
items.abstract: With the continuous development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, smart home systems have gradually evolved from traditional automated control modes toward intelligent systems with environmental perception, autonomous decision-making, and proactive service capabilities. However, existing smart homes still face problems such as a single mode of interaction, insufficient intelligent proactivity, and limited scene adaptability. Based on relevant research results in recent years, this paper systematically reviews the application progress of AI technology in the smart home field, focusing on key directions such as the Internet of Things (IoT) architecture, multimodal interaction, intelligent decision-making, edge computing, and data security. The review shows that AI technology has effectively improved the perception, interaction, and decision-making capabilities of smart home systems. Among these technologies, large language models (LLMs) enhance natural language understanding and user interaction capabilities, edge computing improves the real-time response efficiency of the system, and technologies such as blockchain provide new solutions for data security. At the same time, smart homes still face challenges in privacy protection, model reliability, cross-device collaboration, and standardization. In the future, modern smart home systems should be further integrated with artificial intelligence technologies, change traditional basic interaction modes, and promote the development of smart homes toward greater intelligence, security, and adaptability.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Adaptive Controllers for Resilient Unmanned Aerial and Unmanned Ground Vehicles Cooperative Systems: A Mini Review
items.abstract: Teams of cooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) are becoming crucial in scenarios where their complementary mobility, sensing capabilities, endurance, and physical interaction are beneficial. While UAVs offer fast aerial inspection and flexible perspectives, UGVs ensure large payloads, extended operation time, and the ability to intervene from ground level. Nonetheless, reliable UAV–UGV cooperation is challenging due to different dynamics, occasional communication, limited computational power, uncertain environments, and severe constraints on energy. This updated mini-review aims to bring together state-of-the-art and peer-reviewed research on using artificial intelligence (AI) for enhancing adaptive controllers in air-ground cooperation problems. This paper addresses four interconnected topics: learning-enabled control, model predictive and hybrid AI-model predictive control controllers, resilient coordination considering limited communication, and energy-conscious mission planning. As opposed to UAV–UGV surveys, this paper highlights the control-related aspects of air-ground cooperation, which include learning policies, constraint satisfaction, task allocation, degraded communication-based re-planning, and energy-dependent rendezvous. The revision significantly improves the process of selecting relevant literature, eliminates claims on benchmarks without evidence, updates unverified citations or references unrelated to the work, and produces publication-quality graphics. Ultimately, the review suggests that robust implementation would require explainable AI, rigorous sim-to-real transfer techniques, standardization of heterogeneous benchmarks, and efficient lightweight algorithms suitable for limited resources.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Cardiac Magnetic Resonance in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Diagnosis, Phenotypic Characterization, and Risk Prediction
items.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disease associated with a broad spectrum of clinical outcomes, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) plays a central role in the comprehensive assessment of HCM by enabling integrated evaluation of myocardial morphology, ventricular and atrial function, tissue characterization, myocardial deformation, and longitudinal disease progression within a single comprehensive imaging modality. However, conventional CMR interpretation remains limited by manual post-processing, interobserver variability, sequence-dependent measurements, and reliance on a relatively restricted set of predefined imaging parameters. These limitations may hinder the full exploitation of the rich multidimensional information contained in CMR datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, particularly machine learning and deep learning, together with radiomics-based quantitative image analysis, provide new opportunities to extend the diagnostic and prognostic value of CMR to extract high-dimensional and quantitative information from cine imaging, late gadolinium enhancement, parametric mapping, and feature-tracking-based deformation analysis. Emerging evidence suggests that AI-enhanced CMR may facilitate automated image analysis, improve diagnostic classification, support differentiation of HCM from phenocopies, enable tissue- and deformation-based phenotypic characterization, and enhance individualized risk prediction. Although several studies have included independent or external testing, many remain retrospective, rely on selected populations or internal validation, and lack prospective assessment of clinical utility. High discrimination performance should not be interpreted as established clinical utility, because calibration, decision-curve analysis, clinically relevant thresholds, and prospective clinical impact remain insufficiently evaluated. In addition, interpretability and clinical generalizability remain important challenges for translation into routine practice. This review summarizes the current role of CMR in HCM and discusses emerging applications, methodological challenges, and future directions of AI-enhanced CMR for diagnosis, phenotypic characterization, and risk stratification.

This chapter examines the approaches and frameworks for integrating AI into the design and performance evaluation of renewable energy systems. Focus is directed towards data-driven enhancement of system components, energy storage administration, and smart grid incorporation. The results indicate that AI integration improves energy conversion efficiency and operational stability while facilitating the shift to cleaner, more adaptable energy systems.

items.title: Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
items.abstract: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered—or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem’s predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

items.title: Aspect–Sentiment Triplet Extraction in Low-Resource Odia Language Using a Tri-Channel GCN
items.abstract: With the proliferation of digital platforms and smartphones, users increasingly express opinions in their native languages through online reviews. However, fine-grained sentiment analysis for such low-resource languages remains underexplored, as most Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) methods target resource-rich languages such as English. To address this gap, we present Odia-TriGCN, a hybrid framework for Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction in the low-resource Odia language. It integrates tree-distance relations (dependency and constituent trees), syntactic dependencies, and biaffine semantic attention to capture rich structural and semantic cues. The model further leverages auxiliary features from an Odia news corpus and cross-lingual supervision using an Odia–English parallel corpus. We also incorporate a customized dependency parser trained on manually annotated data following the Universal Dependencies (UD) scheme, to obtain consistent head-dependent relations. items.title: Assessing musculoskeletal discomfort among head porters in open-air markets in Ibadan, Nigeria
items.abstract: BackgroundManual load-carrying remains common in developing countries and poses significant occupational health risks. However, integrated three-dimensional (frequency, severity, and interference)-based ergonomic assessment of the head porterage job is limited.ObjectiveThis study assesses the distribution of Musculoskeletal Discomfort (MSD) among head porters in selected open-air markets in Ibadan, Nigeria.MethodsA descriptive cross-sectional survey was done among 100 head-porters in Bodija, Oja-Oba, and Challenge markets using stratified and purposive sampling. Data were collected via an adapted Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ) and analysed by descriptive statistics. CMDQ scores for frequency, severity, and work interference were multiplied to obtain composite CMDQ index for each body region, while percentage CMDQ index (%CMDQ) was calculated to rank affected body regions. Data were analysed using chi-square tests and Spearman's rank correlation at a significance level of 0.05.ResultsMost participants were females (78.0%), aged 30-55 years (71.0%), and worked more than six hours per day (79.0%). MSD was widely reported across multiple body regions, with the lower back being the most affected, followed by the left thigh, right thigh, neck, and knees, with %CMDQ of 8.8, 7.8, 7.7, 7.6, and 7.2%, respectively. MSD frequently interfered with work performance and reduced job satisfaction. A weak, but statistically significant, positive correlation (r = 0.31, p < 0.05) was found between MSD severity and daily working hours.ConclusionsThe multidimensional approach provides a comparative empirical framework for prioritising MSD severity across body regions. The high ergonomic risk observed highlights urgent need for targeted interventions in the informal market environments.

items.title: Assessing the Use of Emerging Technologies for Digital Preservation of Indigenous Knowledge among Librarians in Bayelsa State Libraries
items.abstract: This study assessed the use of emerging technologies for digital preservation of indigenous knowledge among librarians in Bayelsa State libraries. The study was guided by two research questions that examined the emerging technologies available for digital preservation of indigenous knowledge and the extent to which librarians utilise these technologies in Bayelsa State libraries. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population of the study comprised librarians working in selected academic and public libraries in Bayelsa State, Nigeria. An online survey questionnaire titled Use of Emerging Technologies for Digital Preservation of Indigenous Knowledge Questionnaire (UETDPIKQ) was used for data collection. A total of 127 responses were retrieved and used for the study. The data collected were analysed using frequency counts, percentages, mean, and standard deviation. The findings revealed that emerging technologies such as digitisation/scanning technologies, institutional repositories, cloud storage systems, digital archiving platforms, metadata applications, social media platforms, automated library systems, multimedia technologies, and internet/Wi Fi facilities were available in Bayelsa State libraries, with a grand mean score of 2.75 on a 4-point scale. However, artificial intelligence tools were found to be inadequately available. The study further revealed that librarians utilised emerging technologies for digital preservation of indigenous knowledge to a high extent, with a grand mean score of 3.43 on a 5-point scale. Technologies such as social media platforms, internet-based technologies, digitisation tools, institutional repositories, and cloud storage systems were widely used for indigenous knowledge preservation and dissemination. These findings suggest that, although foundational digital tools are gaining ground in Bayelsa State libraries, deliberate investment in artificial intelligence capacity is needed if librarians are to sustain and advance current preservation practice. The study concluded that although emerging technologies are increasingly available and utilised in Bayelsa State libraries, challenges relating to inadequate infrastructure, poor funding, and limited technological expertise continue to hinder effective digital preservation practices. The study recommended improved funding for digital preservation initiatives, provision of advanced technologies, continuous ICT training for librarians, improved internet connectivity, and stronger institutional support for sustainable indigenous knowledge preservation

items.title: Association of AI Assistant Anthropomorphism with Occupational Burnout and Self-Efficacy Among Adult Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Relevance. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants in professional settings introduces new forms of human–technology interaction. Perceiving an AI assistant as a human-like partner may be associated with users' confidence in their abilities and various aspects of occupational well-being. Objective. To examine the associations between perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism and employees' confidence in using AI, occupational self-efficacy, and two dimensions of occupational burnout: exhaustion and disengagement from work. Methods. Data from a cross-sectional online survey were analyzed. The initial dataset comprised 704 responses, of which 665 participants met the eligibility criteria for employment and regular AI use. After excluding four respondents who failed both attention checks, the final analytical sample consisted of 661 participants. The mean age was 30.06 years (SD = 7.34). Measures included the Godspeed, AISES, OSS, and OLBI scales. Descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, correlation analyses, and regression models were calculated. The interaction between perceived anthropomorphism and prior experience with AI was also examined. Results. The anthropomorphism measure (GOD_A) was positively correlated with the AI assistance and self-efficacy measure (AISES_AS; r = 0.148, 95% CI [0.073, 0.222], p < 0.001). Correlations with exhaustion (r = −0.010, p = 0.792) and disengagement (r = 0.024, p = 0.540) were not statistically significant. After controlling for AI use experience, age, and workload, the GOD_A coefficient in the AISES_AS regression model was β = 0.070 (p = 0.082). A statistically significant interaction between anthropomorphism and AI use experience was identified (b = 0.114, 95% CI [0.037, 0.191], p = 0.004). Conclusions. Perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism is associated with employees' confidence in using AI, with the nature of this association varying according to prior experience with the technology. No statistically significant direct association was identified between anthropomorphism and occupational burnout. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the psychological dimensions of AI implementation in organizational settings.

items.title: Association of Noise Exposure, Perceived Noise Impact, and BMI on Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Among Chinese Seafarers: Nationwide Population-Based Survey
items.abstract: Background: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a global public health challenge, yet its relationship between occupational noise exposure and perceived noise impact remains unclear. Objective: We characterized maritime noise exposure patterns and examined the associations of noise exposure, perceived noise impact, and BMI with NAFLD among seafarers. Methods: A population-based survey was conducted from March to May 2024 through the China Shipowners' Association. Participants completed a structured online questionnaire. Noise exposure was assessed via self-report, and NAFLD presence was determined by self-reported physician diagnoses based on the 2018 updated NAFLD guidelines. Results: A total of 8143 male seafarers was included, with an overall NAFLD prevalence of 18.5% (n=1503). The prevalence was significantly higher among seafarers with a BMI of 24.0 kg/m² or above (25.9%, n=1261), chronic noise exposure (19.4%, n=1293), and higher perceived noise impact (slightly: 16.9%, n=589; moderate: 19.1%, n=359; significant: 22.5%, n=511). Among seafarers with a BMI of 24.0 kg/m² or above, chronic noise exposure and higher perceived noise impact were significantly associated with an elevated risk of NAFLD. After full adjustment, the combined association of chronic noise exposure and higher perceived noise impact remained significantly associated with increased NAFLD risk, with consistent patterns observed across both workplace and rest area settings. A significant interaction was also observed between rest-area noise exposure and perceived noise impact in this BMI subgroup. Conclusions: Noise exposure, perceived noise impact, and BMI were significantly associated with NAFLD among seafarers. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing occupational health benefits, especially among those with metabolic disorders.

items.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
items.abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.

items.title: Automated thigh muscle segmentation using foundation models: validation and impact of segmentation quality
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to validate a segmentation pipeline for the extraction of volumetric thigh muscle data, investigate the influence of demographics on segmentation performance, and investigate the influence of low-quality segmentations on quantitative performance and downstream metrics. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Manual thigh muscle segmentations on axial T1-weighted spin echo thigh images of 364 (106 training and validation; 258 testing) participants of the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) were used. A trained YOLO (You Only Look Once) object detection model generated labels and box predictions, that were passed to a fine-tuned foundation model (Segment Anything, Meta), which generated muscle segmentations. The quality of segmentations was assessed by two radiologists (none, minor, major issue), and Dice scores and mean bias versus manual segmentations were calculated in the testing dataset. Linear regression was used to calculate the associations of age, sex, and BMI with Dice scores. RESULTS: Dice scores ranged between 0.97 (quadriceps) and 0.89 (adductors). Exclusion of erroneous segmentations decreased mean bias by 0.06 mL across muscle groups; mean Dice of segmentations with versus without major issues was 0.90 versus 0.94. Female sex was associated with marginally lower Dice scores (beta -0.01, 95% CI: -0.02, -0.01, p < 0.001), while no other demographic feature showed significant associations. CONCLUSION: Foundation models can be fine-tuned on a modest task-specific dataset to achieve segmentation accuracy comparable to bespoke networks, without training a dedicated architecture from scratch. Visually erroneous segmentations introduce only negligible degradation of quantitative performance and downstream metrics and may thus be challenging to identify by data-driven detection strategies. KEY POINTS: Question Foundation models can be efficiently leveraged for robust segmentation on complex thigh muscle anatomy Findings Radiologist-identified erroneous segmentations introduced only negligible degradation of summary quantitative performance and are thus difficult to identify using statistical methods. Relevance statement Human-in-the-loop quality assurance post-validation adds limited value to improve downstream volumetric muscle metrics in foundation-model-based thigh segmentation. These findings carry implications for both research and potential clinical applications of muscle volume quantification, e.g., personalized therapeutic regimens.

items.title: Autonomous AI-Driven Security Operations Centers (Autonomous SOC): Agentic Orchestration, Real-Time Incident Response, and Multi-Agent Defensive Playbooks
items.abstract: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law. Index Terms—Autonomous SOC, Security Operations Center, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), SOAR, Incident Response, MITRE ATT&CK, Dec-POMDP, Defensive AI, Alert Fatigue, Cyber Threat Intelligence.

items.title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

items.title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs
items.abstract: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.

items.title: Balancing Affordability and Accuracy: A Hardware Selection Guide for Wearable Fall Detection Systems
items.abstract: Unintentional falls among older adults represent a severe global health concern, necessitating reliable, automated wearable Fall Detection Systems (FDS). However, developing practical wearable solutions requires navigating intricate engineering trade-offs among diagnostic accuracy, power consumption, memory footprint, and software development overhead. This paper presents a structured hardware selection guide evaluating three representative embedded design paradigms: low-cost threshold logic on 8-bit microcontrollers (Profile A), balanced classical machine learning on standard 32-bit platforms (Profile B), and compressed on-chip TinyML neural networks on edge-capable microcontrollers (Profile C). Comparative analysis reveals that while threshold methods achieve multi-week battery longevity at sub-$12 costs, they suffer from high false-alarm rates during dynamic daily activities. Conversely, TinyML architectures deliver superior classification accuracy (98%) on raw kinematic streams, but introduce steep memory quantization barriers, complex toolchains, and shorter battery recharge intervals. Classical machine learning emerges as the optimal design compromise for most developers, achieving robust diagnostic discrimination (95% sensitivity and specificity) with manageable computational demands at $15-$25. Finally, this review evaluates sensor placement ergonomics, addresses pervasive demographic bias in youth-simulated training datasets, and delivers a practical hardware selection framework for student researchers and independent developers.
